summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31.1965 and March 31st, 1967 respectively) in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,23,790/ representing interest on accrual basis (though not realised) on the outstandings of the money lending business, the accounts of the assessee being maintained on cash basis. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth Tax officer appealed to the Appellate Tribunal and contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the respondent. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellant, but held that accrued Interest was liable not to be added in the Wealth tax assessments. In reference, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The concept of "net wealth" is a well recognised principle of interpretation and it cannot be disputed that the concept of net wealth is not static or static. It has been repeatedly held that the expression "net Wealth" in section 2(q) of the Wealth Act means the last day of the previous year as defined under the Income Tax Act, if an assessment were to be made under that Act for that year; and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. [310C D] 1.2 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee is not a static or rigid formula but has been evolved in many cases to determine the value of assets of an assessee. It is a matter of common knowledge that the business of the assesses is not merely a collection of money but also a realisation of money which is ultimately earned by the business. The concept, therefore, is different from the concept that it is a commercial one and it has been consistently held that in order to determine its value, the value must be determined on a particular date. [321E F] 1:3 In the instant case, the assessee had maintained its books of account in accordance with cash system of accounts adopted by it during that "previous year" stop there. The method adopted by him is not only a collection but also realisation of moneys which are ultimately earned on accrual. It was apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be include within the assets of the an assessee under the Wealth ' Tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts were maintained on Cash basis interest due on accrual base, though not realised, on the Outstandings from the money lent business are liable to included in its net wealth of the assesee. [313C D; 313A B] Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P. I vs M/s. Vysyaaraju B Cadreenarayana (Orissa) (1), and Commissioner of Income tax, A P.I. vs Kigolla Narasimha Rao, ; , referred to. 1:4 The scheme of the wealth Tax Act is that broadly Parliament has fixed upon the last date of the "previous years", as the valuation date. The figure of net assets of assessee at the end of the 'previous year ' takes into account the financial activities of the business during that 'previous Year" takes into consideration the financial activity of the asscssee during that previous year. It does not appear that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by assessee.

The respondent was a workman in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed misconduct and was not found guilty of any misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for setting aside the order of dismissal. The Tribunal held that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained but set aside the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority. The appellant company preferred a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by the Tribu nal on the grounds that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal was based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has no juris diction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere in a case where the Tribunal is satisfied that if some but not all of t he findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable", the order cannot be sustained. [27F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal imposed a lesser penalty on the respond ent. The Court has not gone into the question whether the punishment imposed by th e disciplinary authority can be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the punishment. [28F] 3.2 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings of t his Inquiry Officer are based on the evidence even though some of them may be found to he irrelevant or irrelevant. If the inference that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appellant was too seve rred, it was not for thority to consider any finding on substantial misdemeanor for which t he punishment could lawfully be impose, it has no merits. [29F] 4. The order of the Tribun al imposing a lesser punishment on the appel lant cannot, therefore, be sustained.[30A B] 5. In Shankar Dass vs Union of India this Court set aside t he impugned order of penalty on t he ground that the imposition of the penalty was too harsh to the responde nt. [31F G] 6. The question whether a punishment of dismissing from service passed by an authority can he supported on some finding as regards substantial misdemeano f for which no penalty can lawfully been imposed, is not deter mined in this case since the respondent had already retired from service and his reinstatement in service was not challenged. [32F G; 33A] 7. The res pondent has failed to establish any misconduct or negligence on his part. If it is his case that he was not in fact the person convicted, it would be open to him to challenge the finding of the inquiry officer or the Tribuna nal. [33G H] 8. In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the tribunal imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot, however, be justified. [34F G].

The appellants were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff Inacio Martins who died pendente lite. He had filed a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 1. The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit had been barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968 and hence, the subsequent suit was based on a distinct cause of action not found in the former case and hence the bar of Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The second suit based on the factum of tenancy was dismissed as the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the property in respect of which he claimed to be a lessee. It would have been a different matter if in the previous suit the court had decided the question of status as lessee against the plaintiff, in which case, perhaps it could be argued that the second suit founded on the facts of the earlier suit was not maintainable. The High Court took the view that even after the Fifth Amendment came into force the plaintiff had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of his land within the period allowed by Section 18 of the Act and had, therefore, allowed the first defendant to become a deemed purchaser of the suit property on the strength of his tenancy. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question which arose in the suit is whether defendant No 1 was a tenant or a deemed tenant. [1032C] 1.2 In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenants whose case is not governed by section 8(2) of Act. But in the cases of a deemed lessee who has been evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962 since a remedy has been provided under 1032 the Act, the Jurisdiction of the Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section 58 (2) read section 58(2). [1033D] 2.1 In such an event the remedy would not be one available to the Civil Court to give any relief to the landlord by way of possession of agricultural land. If, on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act, he would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [ 1034E] 2:2 In the instant case, the suit in question was based upon a distinct and cause of actions not found against the appellant. The jurisdiction of the civil court stands wholly excluded by virtue Section 58(1) of Bombay Tenancy Act. Therefore, the question which arises in the present suit was whether defendant 1 was tenant or deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar under section 7 read section 8 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [1004G] 2 :3 In such circumstances, the Civil court would not have been competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant, because it would not otherwise be open to the civil Court to grant any relief in favour of the landlord.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they seek enforcement of their fundamental right to have "equal pay for equal work". The petitioners want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They want the said pay scale of the regularly employed carpent er and painters and carpentors ' helpers engaged in the construction industry. They have also sought enforcement of the right to equal pay for Equal work. The Corporation has clearly stated that there are no regular employees of the petitioners ' categories in its establishment and, as such, the question of payment to the petitioners does not arise. The Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The court pointed out, that principle had to be interpreted into Article 15 of the Consti tution which enjoins that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. It is important to emphasize that equal work for equal Work is a concomitant of Article 14 Of the Constitution. From the averments in the pleadings of the parties it will be clear that the Corporation has no regularly employed engaged carpent ers. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected. [669F H] Randhir Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.

The prosecution case was that on the date of occurrence, the deceased and his wife were staying in a house at about 9.30 p.m. The accused 1 to 3 were armed with deadly weapons and they were armed by their side. They were armed and were armed. On seeing them, the accused persons ran away from the place of occurrence. The deceased was taken to the hospital where he died on the way. The prosecution case further alleged that the accused had assaulted his wife and daughter in a car. The trial court convicted all the seven accused under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for life under section 304 Part II read with Section 34 I P.C., and also to pay fine of Rs. 500/ each, and in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 and 6 for the murder of Malan. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against him in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the High Court of the charge of conspiracy under section 120B I. P. C.; (2) the confessional statement of accused 6 could not have been relied upon as a substantive piece of evidence; and (3) the confession of the accused 5 was inadmissible in evidence because it was retracted from his earlier statement recorded under section 164 Cr. P., which was not admissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused 4 could not therefore be relied on against accused 6 in view Of the fact, that accused 6 had been convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for death under section 306 read with s 34 IP. C., and the confirmation of the conviction of accused 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 by the Sessions Judge under section302 read with S 34 I I.A. could be sustained. [138 F] 2. The confession of Accused 6 was admissible in the trial proceedings as it was not retracted from the earlier statement made to him under section164 Cr.P., which had been recorded under Section 164 Cr P. P, and therefore, the retracted confession of an accused 5 cannot be relied against him. [139 G H] 3. The confessional statement made by accused 6 was inadmissible because it did not contain a recital that the deceased was in any way responsible for the commission of the offence. [140 C D] 4. The confessions of the two accused were admissible in law and could not, therefore, be relied only against accused 1, 6 and 7. [141 E F] 5. The statement made before the police under section 161 Cr. A. No. 348/79 was inadmissible as evidence because the confession was retracted by the accused.

The appellant 's father had executed a will in favour of the respondent, and so Lakshmamma was not competent to make a will. The appellant ' s son died on August 22, 1945, leaving behind his widow, two daughters and one daughter. The respondent filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the will in question was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmma. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the testatrix had no clear recollection as to what happened on the day when she attested the will, and that the evidence adduced by the appellant was highly improbable; and that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the testator fully understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the will. Held, that the High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it was not shown that the propounder fully understood its contents. The evidence of the attesting witness was clearly inconsistent with the appellant ' 's case about previous instructions and so it would be necessary to refer to the broad features, and dispositions of the will and the evidence led by the respondent to prove its execution. The onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending the execution of the document and to establish that Lakshmabai had really understood its terms and put her signatures to the document of his own free will.

The appellant company was carrying on business of sale and sale of Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by the appellant company. The goods were purchased by persons other than those who ran cinemas or for any other use. Of course, it was very difficult to identify a taxable commodity merely by the use to which it may be put. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast, through the projectors on cinema screens and sound recording and reproducing equipment lenses films and parts and accents in a particular area. It also found that the sales tax authorities were compelled to consider the use which is generally made of the arc carbins. The High Court held that these were not taxable under Entry 41 of the First Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. Dismissing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] 2. The definition of "accessory" is not exhaustive in which it occurs in a schedule in which description of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No. 4 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales tax Act, the words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 11 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 12 for dictating, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon are belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. [562 F G] 3. The expression "part" in Entry 41 means that the words used therein include goods as are ordinarily also used for other purposes than as (1) (1965) 16 S.T.C. 862, 966. (2) (1970) 26 S. T.C., 87. (3) (70 I.A. 129) and (4) (1971) 27 S.C . 45.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. [419D] 1.2 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in the public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. [416E] 1:3 The Act was passed for decal opment and development of minor minerals, and for purposes connected there with. Rule 18 of the Rules provides for the determination of the rate of royalty payable in respect of minor mineral. The original rule 21 was substituted by new rule 21 by the issue of impugned notification on 26 6 1985 which provided that a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules shall pay royalty at the rate prescribed for the time being in the rules framed by the State Government in respect o minor minerals except in the case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec tares in the cases of ordinary sand, Kankar Murram Gravel and in the ease of ordinary Sand, Kikar Murram and gravel a lease can be granted upto three years, and the area or land covered by a mining lease is governed by rule 15 which says that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of any specified minor minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction was imposed both on the area in respect to which a Parna could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. [414G H; 414A B] 1 :4 The fact that section 15 of the Act does not authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementing the policy of the statute under which the Rules are made. [413C D] 1.:5 The fact, that section 17 of the Gujarat Mineral Rules, 1966 does not authorize the State Govt. to show any such concession when promulgating rules which are inconsistent with the provisions of Article 301 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying do not involve any movement as such. [ 413D] 2.1 In order to achieve this object, the Legislature has enacted the Gujarat minor Mineral Rules 1967. Rule 21 of the rules provides that a person who takes mining lease or any other mineral conces sion granted under any rule made under sub section (1) shall pay royalties at the rates specified in column 1 of the schedule, removed or consumed by him or by his agent, manager, employee, contractor or sub lessee from the leased area at the Rate prescribed for that purpose. Rule 19 provides for determination of royalty in respect Of minor minerals and for matters connected therewith.

The appellant was the hereditary trustee of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and the suit was not barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the Temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the office of the appellant is hereditary within the expression "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [445 D] (2) The word 'office ' is used in contradistinction to a mere office which may not have been expressly provided for by the founder. It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is an vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [427 E] (3) The appellant must therefore be held entitled to succeed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the second accused, Jabamani Nadar alias Kanyakumari Comrade alias Ramu and also observed that necessarily no case would lie on this kind of testimony against even the absconding accused. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the High Court erred in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness; (2) the evidence of PW 4 is not corroborated by the contents of the FIR; and (3) the medical evidence does not support the prosecution case. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The evidence of this solitary eye witness is not reliable. It is only possible that the court should be circumspect and closely scrutinise the evidence to come to an unhesitating conclusion that he is absolutely reliable. [712 D] 2. The testimony of PW4 in cross examination that when he went near his deceased elder brother about hundred persons were there and "none of them asked him as to how it had happened" appears to be contradicted by the medical evi dence. Another very serious departure from his earlier version is that while PW 4 had stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused Karunakaran as his assailant, this later version appears to he contradicted by his evidence. Another highly serious departure From his earlier statement is that when PW 4 went near the place of occurrence a little earlier than PW 4, did not see the assailants who might have already escaped. It also stands to reason that those persons who gathered would not ask PW 4 who arrived at the place a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. There is considerable doubt as to this testimony with regard regard to seeing the accused running away from the place where he was sleeping to the place when he fell dead. [ 712 E G] 3. The fact that the witness has stated in his first information Report that the appellant was only mention ed the name 'of accused Karunakarhan as his assailants, does not mean that his earlier versions in the FIR stand contradicted by PW 4. If the statement of PW 5 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the scene of occurrence already when he arrived. It may also be conceivable that those person who gathered will not ask him PW 4 for information With regard to see the accused ran away from tho place where they were sleeping to his place where PW 4 was lying.

The respondents were the heirs and legal representatives of one Amarchand N. Shroff deceased. The income was received by the heirs, legal representatives after his death but in that previous year he died. The Income tax Officer found that the respondents had received the salary due to her husband and that the amount was liable to tax under section 24B(1) of the Income tax Act. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment. In reference, the High Court held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by them before his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to income tax under s.24B(2). Held, that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the previous year. The fiction is confined to the case provided in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section 23B. In the present case the fiction was limited to those cases provided by the three sub sections of section 25B and could not be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. Commissioner of Income tax vs Shaw Wallace & Co., (1932) L.R. 59 I.A. 206, referred to. The words "any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs andlegal representatives after their death they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have be liable when the income was receive had he been living.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All non domicile persons were appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra State Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act and the Rules on the grounds that article 16(3) of the Constitution was violated inasmuch as it conferred a power to make laws prescribing conditions for residence in a part of a State. It was further contended that the provisions of the impugned Act were ultra vires the Constitution. Held, that section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957, is intra vires and must be struck down. Article 16(1) of Constitution does not confer a power on the Government to make law prescribing conditions as to residence within the State or Union territory prior to appointment, as a condition of employment in the State, or Union Territory. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. Article 35(b) does not contemplate any discrimination among other things on the ground of residence. It only means that if it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as District, Taluk, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, or union territory, which words mean what they say, neither more nor less. The intention is made clear by the words 'residence within the state or Union territories ' which words means what they says, either alone or less. It follows that section 4 of the , is ultra vires and void.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted under section 51 of the said Act and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the mere fact that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. HELD : (i) The mere fact of possession, according to the appellant, did not suffice to show that the letters were secreted by him. [415 D] (ii)The mere fact, that there is even a long delay of more than three months in deliver ing a postal articles to the postal article does not mean merely that the articles had been stolen from the almirah which was said to have been in his exclusive possession. The mere circumstance that there has been even a lapse of several years in delivering the postal articles by the appellant would not be sufficient to show the nature of possession attributable to him. In such circumstances it is sufficient to point out that he must have utilised the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession, [417 G H] (iii)The fact that the almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the father and since he had the key with him it must be held that he was in exclusive possession of these articles.

The appellant, who was the husband of respondent No. 2, filed a complaint against respondent No, 2 alleging that he had been abused and be laboured by respondent No 3, the Sarpanch of Nyaya Panchayat, Jokha Khas. The Magistrate ordered that the complaint should be treated as a petition under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to proceed with the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court had not properly appreciated the evidence in its judgment; (ii) the Magistrate had wrongly held that the application filed by respondent NO. 2 was not supported by any affidavit sworn to or a certified copy of the order, and (iii) the complaint did not contain the date of the High Courts ' stay order. HELD : The High Court should have taken into consideration the fact that the appellant had stayed proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat when no proceeding was pending before him. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [120D] In the instant case, the appellant was not aware of the interim stay order passed by the High. Court. The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the High Commissioner was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Panchas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him, and it was therefore, chary of finding a judicial officers guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the said order of his High Court.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302, I.P.C., for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at the Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not supported by any medical evidence, and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court had been wrongly rejected by the trial court. HELD : (i) The High Courts erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. [211 G] (ii) The evidence of the approver was corroborated by Paley Singh, P.W. 2 who stated that the appellant had a bath in the Canal at night in the canal and had said that he did not see the appellant in the field on account of the crops being not very high. The fact that he was the sword which was stained with human blood at the time of murder is sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder. [212 B C] (iii) The extra judicial confessions of the accused to the police officer were not admissible in evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on. [213 E] (iv) The statement made by the approver at the police station was inadmissible under section 8 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The statement of a co accused person recorded by the Magistrate was admissible under section 33 of the Act.

The respondent No. 1, a local authority, filed an election petition challenging the validity of the electoral roll on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 (No. 23 of 1956). The Election Tribunal dismissed the petition holding that the respondent No 1 was not prompt in moving the High Court and that the petitioner did not have any objection to the inclusion of his name in the electoral rolls on October 19, 1978. On appeal by special leave, the High court held that respondent No 2 had asked for a further direction to be issued to the respondents to refrain from conducting the poll on December 31, 1978, and directed the issue of notice of the petition and stay application to the Respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the Rules. The High Court also held that the writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the period of 20 days had been fixed for entertaining claims and objections, a large number or people who could have filed claims and objection were prevented from preferring them within 30 days from the date of publication of the notice under Rule 3(1), the High Commission had no jurisdiction to do so. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The power of the High 'Court under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High, prima facie, is satisfied that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate delay, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue has been brought to its notice by the petitioners immediately after it was noticed by them. [497G H] 2. The powers of the Court under Article 227 of the constitution to issue any appropriate writ are discretionary and when the High/Court finds that there has not been satisfactory explanation, it is reject ed. The final electoral roll was published on November 16, 1978 and it was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 but before December 25,1978, a few days thereafter, for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under Rule 5(1). The writ petition itself was filed on December 28, 1978 for the second time that the names of 34 persons were received by the Deputy Collector and that was rejected by the authorities concerned. [498A B] 3. In view of the fact that the period mentioned in the notices issued under rule 4( 1) of Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication) Rules, 1963 has been adjourned twice before, it cannot be said that there was any satisfactory explanation from the petitioners for the inordinate delayed filing of the writ petitions.

The first respondent company was incorporated in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The company had its registered office at Madras and its registered offices were situated within the limits of the State. In the year 1967, the company closed down its business and started functioning as a stockist under the name and style of "M/s. Vulcan Industries (P) Ltd., Madras. On October 30, 1967, it was found that the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section, was not laid before a general body, but copies thereof were forwarded to the Registrar of Companies for being filed with the Registrar. The first respondent Company filed a complaint against the appellants and its directors for failure to Me with the requisite Registrar of companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, which is alleged to have been committed by them in violation of section 220. The appellants contended that the complaint was barred by limitation as the period of limitation had expired on October 30. 1967. The trial court dismissed the complaint holding that the complaints were barred by time and that the limitation had not expired on the date of filing of the complaint. On appeal, the High Court held that if no balance sheet is laid before the general body there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 221 and though wilful omission to call a general meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit account before the company may expose it to punishment udder under other provision of the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In this Court, HELD : (1) The view taken by the High Courts that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134 of the 1913 Act is correct. [437 B] (2) The fact that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meetings. But section 134 lays down that after balance sheet, and profit or loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid before it three copies thereof shall be filed with Registrar. If no balance sheets are laid before any general body the same cannot be heard to say in defence to the charges brought against him that because the general meeting had not been called, the balance Sheet and profit loss account could not be laid before them. [414 G H] (3)(a) The words "in default" occurring in section 134(4) of Companies Act are wide enough to include within its scope a continuing offence also. [416 A B] In the instant case, on principle and authority it should be held that no offences were committed by directors in the present case under sections 134 and 220 of Companies ' Act, and section 220 was not applicable. [420 C D] (b) The word "shall" used in section 135(4), does not mean a mere irregularity or mistake but a mere error or omission to do something which is not within its contemplation. It is clear therefore that on principle the decision must necessarily lead to the conclusion that even in a prosecution under section134 of the Old Companies Act and section 221 of the Indian Companies Act the company and its Directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general Body meeting as a defence to them.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1952. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that the provisions of section 5 (1) were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The object of the Act was that the preamble was to be read as a whole and section 5 of the , did not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to the trial of certain offences. [291 C] (ii) The Special Court had no jurisdiction to try these "cases" of the respondents. The provisions of the section were therefore discriminatory and violated article 14. [292 E F] (iii)The object being, as I have said, different ele ments, it follows that the object by itself cannot be the basis of the classification of offences or the cases, for in the absence of any special circumstances which may dis tinguish one offence or one class of cases from another offence, or class of offences and speedier trial is desirable in the disposal of all offences or classes of cases. [293 G] (iv)The Special Court was not justified in holding that section 5 was discriminatory in so as it authorised the State government to direct "cases". The Act did not make any special provision for the speediers trial of those offences and therefore it was necessary to ascertain whether it was actually based on such a classification.

The appellant was appointed as Radiologist cum Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. He continued to hold the post of Radiologist in the said hospital till 1974 when he was promoted as Radiology cum Associate professor of Radiological (ex officio) in the Medical Colleges and treated as an Associate Professor. The appellant 's claim for promotion to the post was rejected by the Government on the ground that he did not possess at least five years teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in the concerned speciality as required under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant holding that the appellant possessed the qualification and experience requisite for appointment to the posts of Associate Professor as he had the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post in the Irwin Hospital which is a teaching hospital attached to the Ma ul Azad Medical college. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The designation of the appellant as a Radiologist Cum Associate Professor in Radiotheology (executive) in Maulana Asian Medical College is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professor or Assistant Professor in a Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and the mere designation of his appellant as such does not give him a right to hold that the post he has been substantively appointed to the said post of Associate professor. [8A B] 2. The status of the Associate Professor (ex Officio) which the appellant holds in the Ultrason Hospital is akin, to that as honorary Professor/ Associate Professor, in the Willing does not confer him a Right to hold his post of Professor of radiotherapy. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that the designation of appellant as Radiological cum Associate Professors of Radiology (Ex officio) by the University of Delhi does not given him a power to hold or to hold any the post or to appoint Assistant Professors and Lecturer respectively in the Specialists ' Grade II for a non teaching job. [884C D] 3. The position which the Appellant enjoys as Radiologists cum Associate Dean of Radiography (exhibit officio) is akin also to that in honorary Professor and Associate Professor/Assistant Professors in the willing donomjang hospital or the Hospital and mere designation does not make him eligible for appointment. [874C E] 4. The post of Assistant Professor of Pathology ( ex officio) which was a teaching post, was a clinical post while that of Associate Dean was a Teaching post. That being so, it was urged that there is a distinction between the two posts of Radiologists and Associate Professors as the post which the appellants hold in the Colonial Medicine and Surgery. The mere designation or the appellant 'as such does cannot give him any right to holding the Post of Assistant Professors of radiological, nor can he be considered eligible for promotion or appointment. By analogy, it would be difficult to support the impugned action of the Government of India in the Health Ministry in holding that teaching experience gained by the Appellant as Radiographer cum Associate Director of Radiographic (ex officio) with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into consideration. [864D E] 5. The question whether a Specialist Grade II in a teaching institution belonging to the Central Government is eligible for being considered for appointment or promotion as a Professor of pathology under r. (2) of the Central Civil Health Service Rules, 1963, as amended by the Central health Service ( Amendment) Rules 1966, and if not, whether the appellant is eligible to be considered for such appointment or appointment, is a question which has to be determined in accordance with law. [854E] 6.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. The first and the main point argued was that casual workers should also be paid minimum wages on the same basis as the permanent workers for whom the minimum wage was fixed by the Tribunal which is being varied by this Court. On behalf of the workmen it was contended that the Tribunal had committed an error of law in fixing the minimum wages in the Company on the basis of the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in that region which, in its opinion, would be appropriate under the circumstances of the case to fix the minimum rate of wages in those industries. HELD: (i) The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and, at the time of reference at least there was not and there could possibly be a claim for higher bonus on the ground that, under the Agreement of 1959, the workmen and the Company had agreed specifically to exclude these classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus. [678 F] (ii) The principle which is applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rate of three months basic wage in each case and in no case is the dearness allowance taken into account. [682 G H] French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs Its Workmen, ; , followed. (iii) In the Aluminium Factory, the number of workmen who have to be paid production bonus is very small and almost insignificant as compared with the number in the company 'In these circumstances, it would be more appropriate to compare the total wage packet of the Company with the wage packet received by the workmen of other industries. [679 G H; 678 A B] (iv) The claim was based on the circumstance that according to the workmen, the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to three months ' basic wages, while, the case of some clerical staff, the calculation was made on the assumption that it would have to he taken into consideration.

The assessee was a partner in a partnership firm. On June 3, 1966 the 1st respondent issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961 calling upon him to furnish within thirty days from the date of service of the notice a return of his income or the income of such other person during the previous year, in the prescribed form and verified in the manner and setting forth such particulars as may be prescribed. The assessee filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said notice on the ground that it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commissioner was satisfied that the assessee had failed to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for that year, income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for the assessment year 19 19. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board of Revenue did not set out any reason for coming to the conclusion that the Income tax Officer had complied with the requirement of section 148 and section 151 (2) and that the notice issued under section 147 was invalid inasmuch as it did comply with all the requirements. HELD : The report submitted by the Income Tax Officer to the Commissioner, it is clear that he could not have had reasons to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of these assessee to disclose truly and truly every material facts essential for his Assessment for that assessment year, the income chargeable chargeable to income tax has escape assessment for any assessment year. [446C D] The report of the Incometax Officer to be vague and indefinite does not mention any reason why he was satisfied with this information in his possession, had reasons or belief that by reasons of the assessee 's omission to disclose full and truly material facts relevant for his assessments for that years income chargeable has escapedassessment for that Year. [427B] The word "yes" is used in section 147(2). It does not mean that it should be construed as a mere possibility or an inference of fact. It means only that the intention of the legislature is to give effect to the intention and object of the legislation. In other words, it must be presumed that the legislature intended to give a meaning to the language used in the statute. [544C D; 548A] The Commissioner has no jurisdiction to issue a notice unders. 148. He did not himself record that he was satisfaction that this is a fit case for the issue of a notice u/s 148.

The appellant was a firm carrying on business in the name and style of Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers, Piece goods and Yarn Merts. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the appellant for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner the appellant contended that as a result of the splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. Held, that the income, profits and gains of the period between April 13, 1939 and March 28, 1939, were not liable to be taxed in respect of the income profits and gain of the year 1948 50. The business was taxed under the 1918 Act while the emphasis in sub section (4) is on succession to a person who, on April J., 1939, was carrying on any business on which tax was at any time charged under the Act of 1918. The mere fact that he was not taken on in the original 'business also shows that the original partnership business in respect Of which alone the benefit of section 25 (3) could be claimed continued uninterrupted. In the present case there is no succession to the business carried on by the appellant. The only question for consideration was whether the income and profits of the previous year should be deemed to have been the income or profits of that period. Held further, that in terms of business in a business sense, and it is the business which was taxed before the benefit could be obtained. The fact that the appellant was not taking on the original day also shows the existence of a family partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son, and he was the assessee 's income.

The appellant, a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener, was born in the year 1947. He had two sons, namely, his two sons and the widow of his two daughters. The first son died in 1954. The second son died on September 1, 1956. The third son died before the coming into force of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the appellant 's mother was the only surviving son. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property claiming that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary and that there were six sharers in the coparcenary properties, that there had been no prior division and that it was not possible for the appellant to get a share therein. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the property belonged to a joint family and that, therefore, there was a prior partition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit property belonged exclusively to the Joint Hindu Mitakshara Family and that in any event, the appellant was entitled only to a half share; (ii) the respondent 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s estate upon his death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The property belonged not only to the coparcenary but also to the widow. [724B] 2.1 A joint Hindu coparcenary is a creature of statute and it cannot be created by any statute. It is not open to the court to create a new coparcenary in respect of the joint property which has been partitioned during her life time between himself and his two wives. [764C D] 2(a) The rule that a coparcener can obtain a share only when he is entitled to claim partition or where there are several coparceners in the family, is not seriously disputed. [774D E] 3.1 In order to ascertain the share of heirs in the property of a deceased coparcener it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain whether a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff 's husband and his sons, two must be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if any, made by the deceased and since there is none in the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act. [754E F] 3(b) The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in a joint Hindu family property upon his birth. [765F G] 4.1 The inevitable consequence of the rule is that if a partition has actually taken effect during her lifetime, it must be presumed to have taken place immediately before her death. If the law provides otherwise, the rule of intestate inheritance contained in section 6 does not apply. [664G H] 4(a). In an important aspect, the case before us is stronger in the matter of working out the fiction because in a partition of coparcenary property, the interest of a Hindu coparcener "shall be deemed to be the share in that property that would have been allotted to him if a disruption of that property had taken place before his death". [723B C] 4.(b) In order that a son may obtain a 1/4th share and two, that the share should be determined by adding 1/3rd share which he would get on his death, it is sufficient to show that the deceased had not been in possession of any share in his coparcenary property because after all the three daughters had become co owners.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were framed by the Central Government under section 11(2) of the Life Insurance Act, 1956. The regulations provided that an employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956 shall retire on completion of 58 years of age but the appointing authority may, if it is of the opinion that it is in the interest of the corporation to do so direct such employee to retire on completing 58 years. The respondent was a member of the Employees State Insurance Corporation and was appointed to service of that Corporation on 1st Sept., 1956. In the year 1965 there were more than 200 insur ities carrying on life insurance business in India. After the coming into force of the Act, the Life Insur ive Corporation of lndia (Staff), Regulations, 1961, framed under section ll(2)(b) of Act, read with the settlement entered into between the respondent and its employees on or about 1st October, 1956, was abolished by the Life Assis tration Corporation. The appellant Corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of Regulation 19(2). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the regulations were not in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees of the respondent Corporation under section l9(2), and that the Regulations were not applicable to them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had the right to continue in service if he had remained in Class III only till he attained the age of 60 years, he could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Regulations are applicable to all employees belonging to class lI and II of the Corpora tion. They are applicable even to those who joined the service after 1 st September 1956. [196B] 2. Regulation 19 is not violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is only in 1965 under the settlement that the age was fixed at 60 years. In order to get over this difficulty, it is necessary to have a rational nexus between the classification and the object to be attained thereby. The Act itself made a distinction between transferred employees and those recruited to the Service of the State on or before 1st April 1956. It does not make any difference whether the employees who were appointed prior to 1st August 1956 were transferred to any service of tho Corporation on that date. [197D E] 3. The High Courts erred in striking down regulation 19(1) as amended in 1977 and in directing the Corporation to continue the 1st Respondent in its service till he completed the age Of 60 years.[197F] 4. Regulation 20(2 ) is not repugnant to Article 14 of the Constitu tion. It only provides for a reasonable nexus between transfer of employees and their transfer to the Corporation. [198G] 5. The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 are applicable in respect of the transferred employee and those who entered the service prior to that date by the Corporation in respect thereof. [199B] 6. The Central Government services and the State Government services are governed by the Act itself. It may be so.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India, the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The Chief Justice sent a letter on 20 February 1975 to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice, Haryana High and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab High Court, stating that he had been instructed by the Chief Judge of the High Court to send a notice to the Chief Secretary, Haryana and Haryana high Court for consideration of his apology. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the constitutional validity of the said letter. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the allegations made in the letter were not scandalising the Hon 'ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people ' faith in the administration of justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the contents of the letter which he and others addressed to the Governor of Punjab, the Prime Ministers did not constitute contempt; (2) the allegations in the letters were vague and indefinite; (3) the High Courts had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ peti tion. HELD: (i) The letter in question was addressed by the deponent to the Secretary of State for being handed over to him for his personal attention. [246E] (ii) The contents of this letter constituted contempt of court and not a duty in discharge of office of a Judge nor is it a duty In discharge of his duties, a Judge must go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. However, if the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech.

The petitioner, a company registered under the Indian Companies Act, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49. During the investigation of that case the Income tax Officer found that the petitioner had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thereby evaded tax. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the grounds (i) that the provisions of section 6(4) Of the Act were discriminatory and violative of article 14 of the Constitution, (ii) that there was no substantial difference in the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner 's income and did not affect his liability to pay income tax. Held, that the procedure for reference under section 5 (1) Of section 5 Of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, is substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure provided under the Act in respect of assessment or reassessment proceedings taken under the provisions thereof by themselves form a class distinct from those who evade payment of income tax and come within the ambit of section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act. The procedure prescribed in this matter by the Act was substantially prejudicial and the persons against whom proceedings were taken under section 6 (4) were deprived of the rights of appeal, second appeal and revision conferred by sections 31, 32 and 33 Of the Income Tax Act. Held further, that there is no substance in the contention that the impugned provisions of the impugned section are discriminatory and unenforceable. The provisions of article 20(3) of India Constitution do not offend against article 14 Of the Constitution and are therefore void and unenforceable under article 14.

The appellant, a "commercial establishment" carried on in the premises in question. The Federation was registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. It was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling goods. In the course of its activities, the Federation had been carrying on various kinds of trade and commerce. The Association was formed for the purpose of carrying on certain types of trade or business in connection with, or incidental to, the objects of the Federation. The appellant was a "Commercial Establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act which, in consequence had no application. "The Federation failed to comply with the direction and contended that it was not an "establishment" as defined in section 2 (9) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activities carried on by the Federation were a business or trade. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The definition of "commercial Establishment" in section2(j) of is far wider than that of " commercial establishment". [352A B] 2.1 It is immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial Establishment" because by the Memorandum of Association, Articles of Association and other material, which was more or less the same as in the present case, it was held that these activities of the appellant were also in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'commercial establishment". The fact of the matter is that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Union as set out in its Memorandum of association, and is not distributed among its members. [352C D] 2:2 The mere word "trade" does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the definition of the word "business" in s.2(h) of Act is far narrower than that in section. 2(j). [352B C] 3:3 In the instant case, before the High Court, it had not argued that the activity of the Association was not a "trade", business or profession. The fact that the respondent is a Federation of Federations and not an association of any individual traders, industrialists or businessmen cannot, by any stretch of reasoning, be called a "business". [353C D; 353A] 4:4 In the very definition of a 'commercial Establishment", it indicates that the function of a registered society, charitable or other trust will not take it out of the definition if the activity carried on is a business. It would bear repetition to say that the mere word 'trade ' does not automatically mean something By which a profits is made, and it will bear added that the concept of mere word is used in the Act. [353F] 5:5 The fact whether the activities of a Federation are also in nature of materials services within its wider definition indicates that these activity of a society, Charitable or other Trust will not come within the definition unless the activity carries on business or commerce. It does not mean something which by itself amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R. Mittal 's case, ; , referred to.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in Benaras. The income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. He observed that "in fact this income arose from a statutory obligation of the Government to pay it, and although the Government recouped this from the person with whom the land was settled, land in the genealogical tree of Malikana appears in the second degree, its immediate and effective source is the Government 's statutory obligation to pay the same. The source of the pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the assesse was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. It further observed that the income of trust appropriated by the appellant as remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the income appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. The question referred to the High Court was: "Whether on a true interpretation of clause (viii) Of sub section 3 of section4 of the Indian Income tax, 1922, the sum of Rs. 36,396/ received by assessee as an allowance during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 is revenue income liable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922? " The High court answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the source of his income was clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it was not agricultural income as defined in the Act; (2) the income could not be held to be derived from land within the definition in section 2(1)(a) of Income tax. HELD: (i) The right which was conferred by the letter of July 7 1837 was a right in a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collection after deducting cost of Tahsil establishments. It follows from the decisions of the Privy Council and the judgments of this Court cited above that if it is held in this case that the source was income, the respondent and his ancestors were given an allowance of Rs,. 36,397/ which was not in the right to receive rent or Revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The amount of Rs 36,398/ received as remuneration was not received in cash or kind but was a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the respondent 's predecessor in 1836. [705 C D] (ii) The source and character of income are, therefore, altered when a part of the agricultural income of a trust is appropriated by it as his remuneration, and that is so notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the profits, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. [700 E F] (iii) The income of Rs 26,398 was not exempt from taxation as agricultural income.

The petitioners in the writ petitions claim to have been appointed as Supervisors Gra de 'A ' in various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966 a nd had filed these writ petitions with the prayer that they be granted promotion to higher posts. The respondents in the said writ petitions claimed that they were entitled to be treated as Chargeman II on completion of 2 years ' service as Supervisor 'A and that their promotion thereafter could be effected only in accordance with the normal rules. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the petitioners of this appeal had not been promoted as Chargemen II on expiry of 2 yea rs of continuous service on the basis of the circular dated 6th November, 1962 and circular dated 20 th January, 1966. In the appeals to this Court it was contended for the respondents that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated a post by promotion were to be made on the ground of completion of two years ' servi ce as Supervisor A ' by its order dated 16th April, 1979, there was no scope for automatic promotion merely because some Supervisors having been en promoted as chargeman II and some others had even been promoted to higher post. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants of this case have in purs u ance of the order of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981 been given a back date promotion to the post of Chargeman Grade II on completing two years of service as Supervisors Grade A. 441 of 1981 are disposed of by issuing a direction to the respondents to give them in the aforesaid Civ il Appeal the same benefits as were granted by the Madhya Pradesh High Court to such of the petitioners before that Court wou ld be granted to the 109 petitioners before this Court w ho were Supervisors 'A, and were granted promotion as Chargem an II by its judgment dated 4th April 1983. [441C D] 1.2 The appellants in Civil Appeal No. 441/81 may also be granted the same relief which was granted to them by the High Court. As regards back wages the Madhya Prade sh High Court held that the appellants of the appeal have in due course been en en promoted to the higher post with effect fr om the date their junior was promoted. [442D] 1:3 The appellants have in this case not been able to show any rule or circular which would govern the matter. They have also not been given promotion as chargemen II.1 In view of the fact that they have not been granted promotion, they cannot claim to be deemed Chargeman I on completion o f two years service as Charge man II.2 It is now settled law that there has to be no p ay for no work i.e. a person will not be entitled to any p ays and allowance during the period for which he did not perfo rm the duties of a higher post although after due considerati on he was given a proper place in the gradation list havi ng deemed to be promoted to that higher post though after due consideration o he was give a proper date in theradation list hav ing deemed to have be en promoted. The appellants cannot claim any right to be considered for promotion merely on completion or completion of three years ' services as Charge Man II by their order dated 6 11 1966.
