The Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, the appellant in these appeals, was granted permits for operating in any inter State route. The State Transport Undertaking applied for stage carriage permit from a State Transport undertaking for operating on the route. On the basis of the said application, the State Transport Authority granted permits to the private operators. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the permits and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso to section 63(7) did not offend article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the High court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that the fourth sub clause of the proviso was unconstitutional and violative of article 14. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) does not mean mere passing of an approved scheme or a notification by the State Government to the effect that it would be effective from the date on which the scheme is sanctioned. [1015C] 2. The proviso to sec. 63(1) does no say for example, like section 68 F(1), that the permit shall be granted to the State Undertaking. It only provides that in the case of inter State routes, the Undertaking will have preference in the matter of stage carriage permits. [ 1015C D] 3. The general scheme of the Act in the context of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68F(1)(a) the permit has to be necessarily granted to such State Transport Undertakings in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1005D] 4. The words 'preferably grant ' occurring therein cannot mean mere making of an application for stage Carriage permit from one State to another. It is not necessary that the applicant should have a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(2). [1016E] 5. The expression 'preferential grant ' appearing in section 68D(1H) does mean only an application made for stage transport permit from another State Transport Corporation and not a mere application for a stage carriage Permit. It does not say, for example that like section68 F(I)(a), the permit had to be invariably granted to a State transport Undertaking. [102E] 6. The sub clause (iv) of the provisos to section63(7), is unconstitutional and it cannot be said that the application made by the applicant for stage stage carriage stage carriage was not for tourist vehicles or travel agents. [103F G] 7. The second proviso to s. 63 (7) is unconstitutional, and it is struck down as violative of Article 14 of Constitution. [104G H] 8. The third proviso to sub section (7), does not state that the permits shall be given preference overall other applications. It merely provides for preference to be given under section 47 (1H).

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant under the name All India Trading Company. Purushottam Raju was the sole proprietor of the business and had been assessed to sales tax in respect of his turnover for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 's contention was that the transaction was a sale of goods which were discontinued or the ownership of which had changed. The appellant contended that the State Government had no authority under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act to create a legal fiction by which the transferee of the, business was constituted as the dealer liable to pay the tax in his hands. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Rule 21A is ultra vires as it does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee; and (ii) Rule 22(c) is ultra rites. HELD: The rule making powers of the state Government under section 9 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 are beyond the rule made by the State Legislature either under section 10 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. [665 B] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., ; , followed. Badrida Chetty vs C .I. T., ; and Badridah vs C I.T. (Central), Calcutta, ; , referred to.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra, on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311 (2) and directed that the decree passed by the lower appellate court be varied so as to show that the appellant continued to be in Government service till the date of suit only and there will be a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State of Maharashtra that (1) the High Court erred in holding that there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer before him and (2 ) the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy thereof amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311. HELD : (i) The decree of the High court decreeing payment of arrears of salary is truly a liability in proceedings relating to a contract within section 60(2)(a) of Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. [922 D] (ii) The words 'actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in this context are wide words and include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of pay the decree more properly falls under section 60 of the Act rather than under section 61. [936 D] In the present case there was nothing to show what material was influencing the InspectorGeneral of Prisons. The report of Enquiry Officer did not disclose that he had applied his mind to the report and had given his tentative conclusions. The final conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him, and in depriving the plaintiff of a copy. [946 E] (iii) The High court erred in basing its decision on the report submitted by the Enquiring Officer before it and the tentative conclusions arrived reached by the enquiry officer were binding on the State Government.

The appellants, who were the successors in interest of the respondents, made an inquiry and came to know that the respondents had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached land unworkable. The trial court held that the defendants had encroached on their leasehold land within three years of the date of the filing of the suit, that the suit was not barred by limitation and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. On appeal, the High Court reversed the findings of the trial court and decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pit pit in the encroached area; (ii) article 49 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, applied to a suit and the appellant was entitled to relief under article 48. Held:(i) The High Court erred in holding that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondent beyond the prescribed time was on the appellants. (ii)(a) The onus of proving that he obtained the knowledge of a particular fact within three year of the institution of the action is on the plaintiff and not on the defendant. (b) The appellant gave evidence to show that the encroachment was prior to 1932, but there is no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that the appellants came to knowledge of it only in the year 1941 which was within three months of the said date.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The respondent terminated the services of the appellant under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the termination on the ground that it was mala fide and was not bona fide. The tribunal held that the action taken by the appellant was bona fide and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to inquire into the causes that led to termination of service under r 18(b). The Tribunal has the right to inquire whether there was in fact misconduct or not and if it is satisfied that the act done by the employer was a colourable exercise of power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [824 D] (ii) The appellant had failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of its power was bona bonafide and was in public interest. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the order terminating the services was bona fides. [884 F G] (iii) The employer could defend the action under r, 18(1) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and therefore the action was bona bona fide or was a result Of victimisation or improper unfair labour practices. [894 D E] (iv) The question whether the action of the employer in terminating the service of an employee is bona fide must be determined on the facts of each case. In the present case, the tribunal had held that there were misconduct and it could not therefore inquire into those causes that might have led to the termination of the services under r 17(a). [895 F G; 896 A] (v) The tribunal was right in taking the view that the discharge of the respondent was bona. fide and did not justify before it.

The appellant was the receiver of a theatre belonging to the respondent. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that as sub lessee or licensee under law it was entitled to obtain and remain in possession of the cinema, and that the respondents were estopped from denying its rights to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal in limine. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [445 B] (ii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has recorded a finding that the agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease and that it was not even averred that it had been a lease. The High Court proceeded to decide matters on which no decision was till then recorded by the Trial Court and which could not be decided by the High court until the parties had opportunity to lead oral evidence thereon. [441 G H] (iii) The High court has recorded findings that the appellant was entitled under section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 to obtain an order for exhibiting exhibit motion picture in the cinema theatre under the agreement. [442 C D] (iv) The trial Court had not decided any issues at all. It had also held that the question asked in cross examined by the appellant did not decide any issue at that stage. The Trial Judge was therefore right in holding that the questions asked were already concluded by the consent decree in suit No. 149 of 1960. [443 D E] (v) The order passed by the trial Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as a Pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was working as a pilot Officer. In the year 1972 he was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. The term of the respondent had come to an end on 30th August, 1985 as stated above and no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. In this connection it was contended that the interim order granted in favour of the respond ent was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th of August,1985 were liable to be ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to con tinue till he completed the age of 58 years. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ petition was liable tobe dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was submitted on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24th March, 1988 directed that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled for remain in service and further observed that it was open for the opposite parties to consider the claim of the petitioner for continu ation in service or of fresh appointment and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent had not urged before the High court that the order dated 9th July, 1986 passed in his case was not an order of extension of service. If the respond ed was really aggrieved by the judgment dated 24.3.1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that was not right in making an order on Review on 26.7.1988 relying upon the interim orders dated 10th July 1986 passed by this Court during the pendency of the Writ Appeal. [243E F] 2. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondents were entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the merits of the case and the extent of his right. [244F] 3. The order dated 10.7,.86 passed by High Court on review and restore the Judgment dated 24/3. 1988 passed in the Writ Petitions. The Interim order did neither and could have been amount to an direction that he was not entitled to remain in serv beyond 30th September, 1985 unless there was a further extension. [245G] 4. The writ petition was dismissed by this court on the ground of delay. [246F] 5. In view of the fact that no order of 'extension had been sanctioned by the Government beyond 30.8.1985, the respondent could not have filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Curt. The stay order did nothing but only a direction to the effect that the Respondent was entitled only to remain on service till he attained the age Of 58 years and further directed that he be treated in service even though there was no order from extension of services.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for seven years. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the evidence of P. 1 to 3 was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] (2) In a case where two views are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the possibility of duality of views. [369F] (3) The evidence of the eye witnesses has been corroborated by the evidence given in Court of Sessions. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [370G] Khem Karan & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. (4) The fact that the appellant was a woman of 69 years old, before the occurrence, makes a gesture as if she was stabbing the deceased and that the deceased cried out 'Amma. The Inspector of Police P. W. W, W.W. 1, who was then posted at the house of the accused, prepared by him, prepared the scene of offence which was later taken over by the Inspector of police. He also stated that he went ahead with the further investigation and found the accused lying on the ground in front of the house by means of a rope. The Sessions Judge thought that when there were two conflicting versions given by the prosecution and the defence, the benefit should be given to the accused. [367A B] Khem Chand & Ors vs State, ; , applied. (5) In the instant case, the evidence was corroborated by what was mentioned in exhibit P. 2, the statement of the appellant to the effect that he saw the accused who was sitting by the side of the body on the cot making a gestures as if he was stabbing her and that he had been stabbed by means which he cried. The evidence was not sufficient to entitle an accused person to the benefits of doubt. [366B C] Khem Raj & Ors., vs State Of U.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as an Assistant Sessions Judge in January, 1978. He was removed from his office by an order dated May 27, 1978 passed under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court on various grounds including that he had been removed from service without holding any inquiry or giving him a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and that the order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) Section 6(i)(c), specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 5 of the Act alleged to have been committed by a public servant i.e. the Judge of a High Court, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government; and (ii) that the provisions of sections 6(2) and 6(3) are not applicable to the case of a Judge who is removed from office by the President in accordance with clause (4) of Article 124 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a Judge under section 3(i) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947 is a special law enacted by Parliament under Article 124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [216C D] 1.2 The word "court" in section 6 (i)(a) has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of competent authority under Section 6 of the . [217D E] 1:3. The word 'court ' is not defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure but it has been used in the sense in which it is used in section 2(g) of that Act. It has been held by this Court in State of Bombay vs Purushottam Jog Naik, ; , that a Judge or Chief Justice of a District Court cannot be removed from the office by any other person except by his removal from office in accordance With clause (a) of article 124 and (b) a special procedure enacted by the Parliament under article 124(4) is clearly visualized when the purported misbehaviour is dealt with by the Chief Justice. [217E F] 1 :4. The provisions contained in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 125 read with Article 2(h) of Constitution are clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior judge, except by their removal from his post in the manner prescribed. [218H; 218A] 1 5. The words 'any person ' in clause (e) have to be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. Any provision which cannot apply to the Chief justice of India, cannot obviously apply to Judges of the High Courts or the Supreme court. [220B] 1 6. The expression 'any other person ' has to he given some interpretation which would placed the burden upon the prosecution as a whole and not on the accused who is sought to be proceeded against.

The appellant was a member of the Saha caste and not a member. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground that Abhoy Pada was a person belonging to a smaller caste group within the Sunri caste, and not as a member thereof. The Election Tribunal held that Abhaoy Pa was a "unit" within item 40 of the Schedule to the Order and dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had established that the appellant belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with Sunri Caste, and (ii) the evidence did not establish that the Sahas formed a sub caste strictly so called within the "the Sunri" caste of a caste wholly independent of the Suniti caste. HELD: The correct interpretation of item 40 is that it indicates men of the " Sunri castes but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste groups of Sahas. [391 E] In the present case, the appellant was not a "Unit" and he did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40 though he was a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to that caste. The evidence clearly established that Abhuoy Pas was thinking of that group as consisting of those Sunris who bore the surname Saha. [392 G] In view of the fact that the respondent did not claim that there was within the ' Sunri ' caste, no question of Saha being a distinct class independent of Sunris could arise. L/S5SCI 27 392 If it were right in interpretation of Item 40, then the only question that has to be decided is whether the respondent has established that he belonged to a bigger caste group called Sahas within the expression "excluding Sahas".

The appellant was the tenant of a flat in Bombay. The complainant and his brother went to the appellant 's house for treatment of his failing eye sight and he was found sitting on the ground floor. At that time the appellant asked the complainant to go to the United Kingdom for treatment. On 4 12 1948, the police party who were down below ready for the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 29,500 from the complainant. The police party searched the flat and recovered certain documents. The appellant was charged under section 19(2) of the Act for receiving the sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain ant. The Magistrate convicted him under section 13(1) (i) of Act and sentenced him to one month 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs, 500. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condi tion of the relistance by a tenant of his right as such and that in the present case there was no such relinquishment. HELD : (1) The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of their rights as such. [421 D] (2) The word "relinquishment" was used in the Transfer of Property Act and not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive meaning as giving up of possession of the premises; and he pointed out that if it was intended by the legislature that "reltenish ment" should have the limited meaning sought to be placed upon it on behalf of the tenant, the word "surrender" used in section 108 sub clause (i), of the Transfer Of Property Act would have been more appropriate.

The appellant, a Draughtsman in the State of Maharashtra, was appointed as an Assistant Draughtsman on a monthly salary of Rs. 210/ per month. The pay scale of the post of Draughtsman and Rs. 150/ was revised to Rs. 180/ per mensem. The workmen raised industrial disputes before the Industrial Tribunal which held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. On appeal, the High Court set aside the award and directed the Tribunal to revise the pay scale and dearness allowance and there was no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workman. The appellant contended that the new wage scales had been introduced by way of an incentive to all the employees who were working as Draughtsmen and that the increase in dearness allowance was not justified on account of the fact that the workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid, the Tribunal considered it fair. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Tribunal was betrayed by a curious confusion in accepting the plea of the appellant that a flat increase to the pay of each individual workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. [176B] 2. The Tribunal was clearly betrayed of a strange confusion in acceptance accepting the contention of the respondent Union that a new wage scale had necessarily to commence with figures Rs. 151/ and Rs 100/ above the existing pay scales. Immediately after the award was pronounced, while the iron was still hot as it were, the employees apparently realised that the employer might take advantage of the circumstance that it was not clearly mentioned in the award that all the employee were to get additional pay of Rs 150/ and that, consequently it fell within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. [177C D] 3. The amendment order required the Tribunal, to revise its scales by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res tructuring the scale of pay and never granted any ad interim increase of salary to all employees. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs. 200/ and again after the figures Rs 150 / and Rs 50/ was added to the Pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs 150 per month in the case of other categories to the initial pay in the wage scales pertaining to those categories. [179E F] 4. The award of the Industrial tribunal is set aside and the Tribunal directed the appellant Tribunal to give a flat increased salary on Entry into the Service and res pondent No. 1 would be entitled to get Rs.150/ per day from the date of the award, i.e., from the dates when the new scale was introduced.

The respondent, an award made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award, and in spite of the Award, the appellant paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The Tribunal held that section 2(vi) included wages fixed by an award in an industrial dispute between the employer and his employees and that the refusal of the employer to pay to them wages at the rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the respondents the said prescribed wages. The High Court affirmed this finding of the Tribunal. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The provisions of section 2 (vi) are applicable only to the wages fixed under the award but not to the workmen. [417 B] (ii) The terms in question need not be express and can be implied; but they must be terms which arise out of the contract of employment and since an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. [420 C] (iii) The fact that on references made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have invariably been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore, the basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad that section was not applicable to the case because the wages prescribed by an Award could not be included within the definition prescribed by section 2 of the , before it was amended in 1958. [416 D E] (iv) The effect of construing the unamended definition of wages is that the old wage structure became inoperative and the place is take by the wages structure prescribed under the Award. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties because that, in truth, is the effect of industrial adjudication. [414 E F] (v) The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended section 2. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that, on references by the Industrial Tribunal, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribe by the Award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of Act before it is amended.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed certain offences. The trial Magistrate acquitted him on the ground that he had not been able to prove his guilt and that there had been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate. On appeal by the State to the High Court, it held that proof that the thumb impression in the acquittance roll was that of the appel lant was sufficient when taken along with other circumstances to establish his guilt, and accordingly convicted him both under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. The appellant contended before this Court that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for prosecution under section 196(1), Cr. P.C., had not be obtained under section 198(1). Held: (i) The sanction was necessary under section 195(1)(a) of Cr. The offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery has been brought home to the appellant and he is, therefore, entitled to have it proved beyond doubt that the acts with which the appellant is charged fall within the scope of his duties as a public servant. (ii)The sanction was required under section 199(1); but the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. The fact that the accused did not claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquit tance roll records the payment, and there is in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name. If what appears on the face of the roll is true and whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction then the acts, with which, the appellant was charged fall under the scope oi his duties, and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office.

The assessee was a resident of Travancore State in the erstwhile State of Cochin. The income tax authorities included the profits of the business and assessed them to income tax under section 12B of the Travancore Income tax Act, Travancore. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business losses incurred in the former State could be set off against the business profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the first proviso to section 24(1) of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, did not apply to the present case because the word " income" used in the proviso to sub section (2) of section 14 of the Act did not include business losses which were incurred in British country or in an Indian State and that the words " loss of profits or gains arising from him within the meaning of clause (e) of sub section(2) Of section 18 of the Income tax, 1922, were used in relation to business or vocation carried on by a resident outside India. Held, that the mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be, set off under section 10 must mean business in British Indian States only and not to any other section. The mere fact that the word ' income " is not used does not justify the construction. that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the Indian States.

The respondent company was a public limited company. Its employees were governed by the Calcutta Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and its employees were entitled to retire at 60 on attaining 55 years of age. The workmen claimed that these showed clearly a tendency in the Bombay region to fix the retirement age at 60 years. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix retirement age of 58 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the age for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. [445 B] (ii) The approach adopted by the Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not very commendable and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. The reasons given by the High Court for holding that in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in Bombay area the trend has been to fixing the retirement ages at 60, were wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. [427 C] (iii) The decision of this Court on an appeal must be confined to the facts and circumstances of each case. The first respondent, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was appointed as the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company. The first respondent filed an application before the Chairman for appointment of the second respondent as the chairman of the board of directors of the Company. The Chairman also stated that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellant was being conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members and other persons and further that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs of the companies had in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. The second respondent contended that the Board could not pass an order under section 237(b) of the Act as the first respondent was not a member of the first appellant company. Held: (i) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 (b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman only if he had reason to believe that the circumstances suggest any of these things and not whether they establish any of those things. In the present case the first Respondent did not disclose anything from which it can be said that the inference which he has drawn was based on circumstances present before him. (ii) The Board was competent to delegate its function under section 236(b). The power to order investigation and delegation is administrative in character and that power cannot be delegated by the Board to itself. (iii) The powers conferred on a Chairman are administrative, and that it can only be validly exercise by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Govern ment under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the appellants.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal by special leave it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The conviction was correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence strengthens the other evidence already against him. It is legitimate therefore to raise the presumption in this case that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. [724 D E] In the present case, the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market and they have been presumed to be involved in the dacoity itself. The time gap is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 E F] In this case, there was no other evidence in the present ease which points to the complicity of the 14 appellants in the crime of dacoity and therefore as they cannot be suspected to be dacoits themselves, the only presumption to be drawn is one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property which was stolen in a dacoity.

If the Government thought in the circumstances that the posses sion or sale of the same is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. [227F G] 5. The State Government by Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by the following Rule: "13 (1) All poisons kept for sale by any licence holder under these rules (except those kept by a chemist, druggist or compounder for the purchase of dispensing or compounding in compliance with the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner) shall be detained in a box, receptacle or building (according to quantity maintained), which shall be secured by lock and key in a Separate receptacle of metal, metal and earthen ware. (2) All 'poisons ' mentioned in clause (x) of rule 2 shall be retained in a room or buildings (according t o quantity maintained) which shall he secured by locks and key and in which no sub stance shall be placed other than poisons, possessed in accordance with a licence granted under the provisions of the .

The assessee firm was carrying on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal for a statement of case on the following question: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable in the books of accounts was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the Department and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending, and (2) the Tribunal had erred in disallowing the claim of the appellant for the balance of Rs 2, 68,385. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has found that the monies were not loans made in the ordinary course of business of appellants ' firm. [10 E] (ii) The finding of the Tribunal is binding on this Court and it cannot be said that the Tribunal erred in allowing the claim for the entire amount of Rs, 2,69,385 as a bad debt. [11 D] (iii) The expression "accommodation" has been defined in section 10(2)(xi) to mean any building or part of a building which is used principally for residential purposes and includes any accommodation intended for residential or other purposes. The word 'accommodations ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules made thereunder. [12 E] In the present case, the Tribunal has held that the amounts were not loan advanced by the appellant to the Bombay firm. It is true that the amount was paid to the assessee as loan and it was not shown that the said amount was borrowed for a purpose other than money lending. But the fact that the assessee had made an application to the tribunal under section 66(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922 to submit a statement on the question "whether on the circumstances and in its circumstances of this case the disallowance of the bad debt of the Rs.2,68.385 was justified in law" does not mean that the debts were not advanced in the normal course of the money lending or that they were not repaid by the Bombay Firm. [13 E F] (iv) The tribunal has found on facts that the moneys sent by the respondent to the High firm were not ' loans made for the purpose of advancing the financial crisis, threatening it in Samvat Year 2007, and that the transactions were totally unconnected with the normal business of their firm. The Tribunal had found that monies sent by them were not debts owed to the appellant.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners challenged the acquisition on the ground that they had not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act and that the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. The High Court granted interim stay of dispossession in respect of the said lands. In these appeals by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that as the awards in these cases have not been made within one year of the date of the notifications making the declarations under section 6 of the 1894 Act, the entire acquisitions had lapsed and that they were entitled to relief under Article 136 of the Constitution. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [565D] 2. The facts of the case are highly material. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [567F] 3. In view of the provisions contained in section 11 A of the land Acquisition Act to which we have already referred, it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material and the petitioners had failed to make out a case for relief. The non disclosure was very material in their determination only when the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. [568F G] 4. The order of the State Government granting interim stay is not vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [569B C] 5. In the instant case, the petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984 and obtained an injunction order of dispossession therein. [570F G; 568A] 6. The orders of the Government granting stay of further proceedings in respectof the acquisition of the aforesaid lands are set aside.

The appellant bank was a nationalised bank. The workmen were drawing basic pay at the rate of Rs. 250 per month. The Sastry award provided that the workmen would be fitted in the new scales of pay from January 1, 1962 on stage to stage adjustment basis, i.e., workmen who entered service of the bank before 1st January 1959 shall not be reduced in any case. The appellant bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the award and also the validity or otherwise of the Sastry award. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Sastry Award provided that "the workmen would work in the old scales of Rs 250 per year as on January 1 1959, and that they would be entitled to increments under sub cl. (a) of cl. 182. Held, that the High court was right in holding that it had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ application. The award provided for a revision of the existing scales of dearness allowance and the revision of pay scale. The revision of scales of Dearness Allowance and the revisions of pay scales were not governed by the Sastry Awards Award. The Desai Award provided for revision of existing scales and the revised pay scale was to be fixed as on February 1, 1959. The scheme of the Desai award was that the scales of allowances in the existing grades would be revised from time to time. The variation in the scales was not a matter of course. It was only with reference to the scales which were earlier fixed by the Desai Award. There was no provision for revision and it was not open to the Sastry Tribunal to revise the scales. The present case was covered by cl. 5. (ii) of the National Industrial Tribunal (Bank Disputes) Award, the adjusted basic pay in the revised scale was not to exceed what point to point adjustment would give an employee on January1, 1959, as modified by placing him at the stage in the Sastry awards scale equal to or next above his basic pay as on 1st February 1959.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain land in Calcutta, applied for a lease of the land on the ground that the Zoo could not be run for a single day without the essential services which were being provided in the four acres of land proposed to be given for the hotel. The respondent State Government granted the lease of Begumbari land to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of Five Star Hotel. The appellants challenged the validity of the lease on the grounds that the decision to lease the Begumbar land to them was taken on February 12, 1981 and that the said decision was arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The Division Bench held that the Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo when they decided to grant four acres out of four acres. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the interests and the requirements of the Zoological Garden were totally ignored and not kept in mind while passing the decision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Government was very alive to this need for the expan ny of theZoo when it decided to lease a land to respondent No. 2. [263G] 1.2 In view of the State Policy, there would be no question of any resin being sold in the open market. the object of the Government in such a case is not to earn revenue from sale of resin, but to promote the setting up of industries within the State and invite those interested to come up with pro posals for the purpose. The object of State in such an event is not only to earn revenues from sale or distribution of resin but also to promote setting up industries within tapping contract simpliciter there can be no doubt that the State would have to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public interest. But in a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging setting up otheuuu uries within the state, we do not think the State was bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the tapping contracts simpliciter there could be no objection being taken by the Government as a policy decision to the hotel group to start a Five Star hotel. [264G H] 1:3 The land allotted to the Hotel was, as we have seen, not used for the main purpose of the hotel for the establishment of a Five star Hotel, which according to the Government, was a prime need to the city of Calcutta. The land allotment to the hotels was, therefore, as it was not used in the main Zoologyogical Garden. [267A B] 1 :4 In the face of all this material, we are satisfied that the facts and circumstances brought out by the appellants do not justify an inference that the construction Of the pro posed hotel in the Begambari land would interfere in any manner with the animals in the Zo for the construc tion of a five Star Hotel, and the birds arriving at the Zira or otherwise disturb the ecology: The proposed hotel is a Garden hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and dumping ground for rubbish. [268C D] 1.:5 In view Of all this, the State Government was bound by the assurance of the Chief Minister that facilities would be provided for the Zu logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters. The matter was taken in appeal.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, had two houses in Calcutta and the relevant date of valuation was 31st March 1957. The assessee had directed the company to debit his account to the extent of Rs.50,000. On 1.1.1957, the assessee made a gift of Rs 25,000 from his account. The gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's personal account in the books of account in respect of the firm whose accounts were said to be credited or debited. In the case of banking companies or other firms and companies who have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. The Income Tax Officer held that there was no valid gift of the principal amounts as there was a valid gift and therefore the assessee did not make any valid gift. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In reference, the High Court held that the gifts were valid and the interest paid in respect thereof could not be included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [130D] 2. In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in the accounts of the account in his books of accounts would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor. [131E F] 3. The fact that the assessee had made a valid gifts of Rs 50,000 to his son and to his wife respectively did not indicate that he was entitled to retain the possession and enjoyment of the property to tho entire exclusion of the donee or, to the entire exclusion from the exclusion of donor or, as the case may be. [132F G] 4. The entries in books of a bank by credit and debit, do not constitute valid gift but only make it clear that the transaction was genuine and there was nothing in them which could be said to have been credited in the account of the minor donees. [133G H] 5. In view of the fact that there is no registered deed and as there is a book entries in respect to the firm, the question whether there was valid gift or trust in respect thereto does not arise. [134A B] 6. The question whether the assessee has made a proper gift or a trust in favour of his son or relatives is a matter which must be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case. [135C D] 7. In order to find out whether there is valid gift, the Court has to consider the effect of the entries in a particular book by credit or debit, and it is not necessary that the entries should be made contemporaneo nately or with such alterations as may be necessary for the purpose of ascertaining the real intention of the parties. [136E F; 137A] 8.

Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The compromise deed is genuine and legal and the same has to be acted upon. [540C] 2.1 In view of the fact that there was the allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to the property which too we have not gone into, it cannot be said that the alienes had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and they had even maintain that there has been improvements by the transferees. [541D] 2:2 The alienee has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to 21.8.1987. The alienation was, therefore, valid and none of the sale deed is valid and no one has any interest in it. The transfereeees have admittedly been in possession of the land from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. The workmen of the Company were granted sick leave for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen. The workmen, however felt aggrieved because of the first proviso to section 49 of the , filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the award on the ground that the Tribunal had given the benefit of sick leave and that the workmen did not deserve any relief for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's awards in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had not given any reasons for allowing the benefit to the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in view of the second proviso to Section 49 of The Act and that since the Tribunal has corrected under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefit which the Act allowed for as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and did not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on Full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal has committed an error in allowing the relief to the workman. [864C] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal was under a misconception that 86 the sickness benefits would be lost for the second two days also. It is not necessary that in the circumstances of the case, to award the benefit, the sick Leave with retro grative effect should cease to applied when the benefit is last paid. [874D] 2:2 The Tribunal had correctly examined the matter and given adequate reasons for awarding the benefit. Such a leave could not be categorised as privilege leave as, by its very nature, it would be admissible only in the cases of actual sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner. It appears, however, that it was not necessary, in the facts of the present case to award benefit of the sick leaves with retro modtive effect on January 1 1975 in the garb of sick. [884E F] 2 :3 The Tribunal ' has cor rectly considered the controversy and given sufficient reasons for granting the benefit under 7 days Sick leave in the manner set out in the award. Such leave could be treated as privilege Leave as, By its very nomenclature, it is not a privilege leave. It was not permissible to give any reason for allowing sick leave without retro specious effect from time to time. [894G H] 2(a) The Tribunal should have given the benefits under 7 months sick leave in view Of the fact that the company had cor rected under the mistaken impression that 86 sickness benefit would be loss for the 1st two days. It has also correatedly examined whether the workmen were entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, and give adequate reasons therefor. Such an leave could only be categorised in the category of actual illness certified by registered medical practitioners. [904G] 2.(b) The High court was not justified in allowing a benefit of 7 days sickness leave as it would amount to granting privilege leave on half emoluments during that period of his physical incapacity.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , on the ground that he had carried on espionage activities or the details of financial aid received by him from the Portuguese authorities or the names of any of the so called underground workers alleged to have been collected by him or made available by him to the Portuguese Government. The grounds furnished were not specific and no particulars of the activities alleged to be carried on by the appellant were given, viz., the particulars such as the length of period for which the petitioner was alleged to had carried out by the petitioner from the French authorities or names of persons aiding the said petitioner or any details of intelligence alleged to he collected by the petitioning authority. The High Court dismissed his application under article 226 on the grounds that (1) the detaining authority did not disclose the particulars of activities alleged by him and (2) the grounds were vague requiring some clarification. Held, that the right to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) whereby disclosure of facts considered to be against public interest cannot be required. The right of the detenue to be supplied particulars, is subject, subject to limitation under Article 22(5), whereby disclosure is of facts consider to be prejudicial to public interest. The power not to disclose facts considered against public interests cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. If the detenue was furnished information at least to that extent, it will enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act for their own information and consideration. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right to representation and An obligation to supply cannot be inferred in these circum stances.

The respondent was a member of the Army Staff. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted by a General Court Martial, and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. The Central Government directed removal from service of Capt. section K. Rao under r. 14 of the Indian Rules 1954. The Chief of the Air Staff, after going through the proceedings of the Court of Inquiry, considered that the trial of the officer by a general Court Martial was inexpedient and he ordered administrative action to be taken under r, 14 of Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1959, an order was passed removing the respondent from service. Rao thereupon filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from the service on grounds inter alia that r.14 of the Defence Rules, 1955, was ultra vires the , and that he should be dismissed from the services. The High Court allowed the petition holding that r 14 of Defence Rules 1954, was intra vires the . Held, that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes it clear that there must be rules, and subject to the provision of the Act, such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the serv ice. The two sections 19 and 45 of the , are mutually exclusive. 14 Of the Army Rules 1954 is not ultra vires. It was argued that the expression "subject" occurring therein in section19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Govern ment has thus no power to remove a person from the Service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. The words "Subject to the other provisions of the . Act and such rules , the Central Govt may dismiss, or remove" in section 21 of the read with r. 15 of the Rules are not ultra Art. 14.

The appellant was assessed to octroi duty under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court challenging the levy of octroi duty on the ground that it was not imported into the limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale and that the appellant had failed to fix the octroi limits in accordance with law. The High Court held that the tax was not validly levied by the Panchayat as it had failed before the Standing Committee to fix octroi limits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 5 of the Taxes and Fees Rules framed under section 3(b) of the Act provides for appeals against levy or imposition of any tax or fee. The appellant has not shown that the Panchayat Samiti or the Standing committee had found sufficient facts to enable it to deal with the question. Therefore, the High court was right in holding that the levy was illegal and ultra vires. [222 B C] (ii) Rule 3(a) does not require the Panchayat to fix its octroi limits for consumption use or Sale. The expression "taxes on pilgrims" is used in a wide sense and includes all taxes levied and collected by a panchayat. The word "tax" has been defined in section 2(11) of C. P. & T. Act, 1947, as meaning the levy or collection of any duty or fee or tax. Therefore the fixing of the octroi limit with the approval of the Collector is an essential condition precedent to the levy and the rules are not confined to octroi duties only. [223 E G] (iii) Rule 4(b), which authorises the levy is r. 22, does not contemplate that the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 should be followed before the octroi duty can start being levied. The fixing of octroi limits with the sanction of the Government is an important condition precedent for the levy. [225 B] (iv) Rule 6(b)(i) does require the Panchayats to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the Rules. The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the Company but in its order they have given very scanty facts and did not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. [226 C D] (v) Rule 7(b). of the Rules requires that the notice following the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax, or fee, should be published by affixing a copy thereof in the office of the panchayat. If so read, it would mean that before the Octroi duty can commence being levied, r. 21 must be complied with.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government and that as 14 days had expired before March 18, 1952, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the meaning of section 12(6) of the Act. Held, that the provisions of sub section 2 Of section 20 of the , are applicable only when a report is received by an appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings therefore do not end when the reports under section 12 (6) are made by the Conciliation officer but when that report is receives by the Government, the appropriate government has to make its report within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the State Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., ; , referred to. The provisions of section 20(2)(b) of Act 2 Of 1952 are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. All conciliation proceedings under this sub section shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when the Report of the Advisory Officer is received and the report is sent by the Inspector to the appropriate Govern ment. Colliery Labour Union Asanso vs Newerson Bissur Railway Co., , referredto. The Act does not affect the jurisdiction of the Industrial Tribunal under section 20 (2)(a) of that Act.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the . The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing on 24th December, 1985 on Katras Coal Dump and the petitioner started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish the criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. In those circumstances it appears that the grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. It further appears that after the order of detention was passed and before the actual service of the detention order, the petitioner was taken into custody. From the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenu or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles laid down in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and particularly in the decisions, in Rameshwar Bengal Shaw vs The District Magistrate Etah & Ors., ; , and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate Etah & others, though there was a statement to the effect that the petitioner 's brother and the detenu had been in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. In these circumstances it is not possible to sustain the order passed by the detaining authority under section 2(2). The continued detention of the petitioner under the Act is not justified. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. In the instant case when the actual order of deten tion was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there were such a possibility of release was taken note by the Detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service of detention order. The order of preventive Detention when it was passed was not invalid and on relevant considerations, the service was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the petition it is nowhere stated that the detenu has since been released or whether the prospect or his imminent release was properly considered by the appropriate authority in the context of the relevant factors. The detention order therefore, is set aside. If however, the detenue is released on bail in the aforesaid criminal cases, the matter of service of order of the deten tion order under the act on the aforesaid materials may be reconsidered by the Appropriate Authority in accordance with law. There will, however, be no orders for release of detenu.

The appellant, a manufacturer of gold trade, was carrying on business as a money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business. The Administrator granted permission to carry on his business under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 for the period from 1st April, 1969 to 31st March, 1970. The appellant challenged the validity of section 28 on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the Administrator could be exercised and that the section confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The High Court struck down the aforesaid provision only on the grounds that it suffered from the infirmity of excessive exercise of legislative powers inasmuch as the Administrator had no power to refuse permission or grant permission. In these appeals by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that section 28 confers an uncanalised and arbitrary power without anything more than any criteria or guidelines for guiding its discretion; (2) that the Administrator is given unlimited authority or power to decline permission or to grant permission; (3) that in making his orders he has regard to the policy and purpose of the Act in making its orders. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The object of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the various restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. [755C D] 1.2 The policy and the scheme of the impugned Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Acts afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [758E F] 1:3 In the absence of parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity cannot be invoked. [759D E] 1 :4. The object and scheme of section 5(1) of the , is to ensure protection of circum potances of the persons engaged in gold trade. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the said premises in that premises in connection with which he carries on business in as such dealer. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on his trade as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policy, and purposes of the enactment and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other provision of the statute shall not be premitted. [761G H] 1.:5. The objective, the policy & the scheme affords sufficient guidance for the Administrator to exercise his discretion in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under section 5 (1). [759E F; 759A B] 2:6. While conferring power on the Administrator under section 4(1), the Administrator was required to have regard to, the anticipated demand, as estimated by him for the ornaments in that region but the expression 'anticipated demand ' was really vague and incapable of assessment leading to a great deal of uncertainty; similarly the expression (1 )AIR 1971 Patna, 240. 112.

The appellants were the trustees of a temple. The properties belonged to the temple and they had been claiming beneficial interest in the property. They claimed that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial court held that the lands had been granted in Inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavar by the Carnatic Rulers before the advent of British power in India and that they had acquired title by adverse possession prior to 1 1 1929, and that the appellants were not holding the same as managers of the trust. The lower appellate court found that the new article was not retrospective in operation and that if the title of the alienees in regard to 'dharmadlayam properties had been acquired by adverse Possession prior to January 1, 1929, it would not be affected by the provisions of article 134 B. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question as to whether on facts proved in the present case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed, is a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title had not been lost by adverse posses sion before the suit was filed. [419 C] (2) The appellants were claiming beneficial interests in the properties all along and that there was no escape from the conclusion that more than 12 years have elapsed since the date of the removal of the previous managers who transferred the properties in question; and so, if a suit were brought by respondents 1 to 3 on the date when they were appointed trustees by respondent No. 1 on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowment, the transfer was void ab initio with the result that the possession had been taken over by other persons who are acting as de facto managers of temple de jure, has not been discussed by the High court. [420 D] (3) The fact that the alienor is still alive, and so it thought that the plea of adverse possi sion could not be sustained. [416 E] Gnanasambanda vs Gnanagambandapu, I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant firm was carrying on the business of cinema business in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu was granted by the District Magistrate in favour of the firm. The firm applied to the District Magis trate for a renewal of the licence. The District Magistrate rejected the request on the ground that the licence had been granted to the firm and that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the High Court. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Government against the order of the District magistrate. The State Government dismissed the appeal holding that the renewal of a licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, the licensee, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Govt. and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ appeal filed by the firm against the orders of the Sub Divisional Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence which could be made only in the names of the original licensees, namely the licensee and there was no mention at all of the partners of the Firm or its partners. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Sub Divnt Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [578F] 2. The licensing authority has no power to suspend the licence which can be made under section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authori ty had no jurisdiction to suspend it. [579A B] 3. The only reason stated by the high Court for quashing the District Commissioner 's order is that the District Magistrates had no authority under the . Act or Rules to make such an order. [580C D] 4. The power to suspended a licence is conferred only by section 6F of the , as one implied in the wider power of revoking and unless there is any provision in the Act, the rules framed thereunder cannot be deemed to have been repealed. [581D] 5. The mere fact that the licensee has been declared an insolvent or a person holding an office under him does not by itself make him a party to the proceedings for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the license and answerable to the licensing authorities for all commissions and omissions in the cinema premises. [583E F] 6.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain properties in Pakistan, applied to the Custodian for cancellation of a lease granted by him under section 12 of the , and called upon them to show cause why they should not be evicted. The respondent contended that the notice was ultra vires the powers conferred on him by section 10 of the Act as it applied only to properties of the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself, and that the direction with reference to them were unauthorised. Held, that the power conferred on the Custodian under section 10 is absolute and unqualified and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The right of the appellants to have their rights determined by the notice dated December 2, 1954, was not affected by the amendment. The notice in terms refers firstly to the lease which it is proposed to cancel and secondly to the movables in respect of which certain directions were given. In the present case the notice did not purport to cancel the agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them. The appellants had no authority under section 9 to issue any direction with regard thereto. The power conferred by section 12 was absolute and that it cannot be exercised notwithstanding anything contained therein in any law for ' the timebeing in force. The right to have the rights determined or varied by the rules made thereunder is subject to the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The Custodian had the power under section 11 to cancel a lease, and the notice could not be challenged on the ground that it was ultra rites.

The appellant, a minor son of the respondent Board of Revenue, was assessed to land revenue by the Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972. The revision application filed by the respondent was dismissed by the Board of revenue on the ground that the land in possession of Raghubir Singh was ancestral and not ancestral. The appellant preferred a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and remanded the case to the Sub division Officer for fresh determination of the call area afresh. The Board ofRevenue, however, held that Surendrapal Singh (appellant) aged 12 years was a minor daughter of Raghubir singh and used to study in Punjab and further held that the respondent 's land was ancestral. In the ultimate analysis the Member of the Board found that there was a gross and patent illegality in the order of the SubDivisional Officer and, consequently set aside the order dated 5th May, 1976 and remanded it for fresh decision.
