The matter was taken to the Board by a revision application and the Board directed that the ceiling area for Raghubir Singh may be determined according to the old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to new law i,e. In 1955. The High Court also did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it decide it in the light of the observations of the board. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 221 of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1950 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and there is no section like sub section (2) of Section 224 of the government of India in the Act of 1935 in the State of Rajasthan. [728D] 1.2 The Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. In order to be a proper and effective instrument for the purpose of better administration, it is necessary that the Board should have been given an opportunity to show cause why the ceiling limit should not be enhanced or altered. Section 221(1) of the Act provides that the State Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. [700E] 1:3 The Board 's power under section 9 is similar and there are no sections like sub sections (2), (2). [730F] 1 :4 In the instant case, the Board had by its order dated 14th April 1975 directed that "the ceiling area may be fixed according to old law". The High court also did neither go into nor did they decide it. It was for the Sub Divi sion Officer, who committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Boards of Revenue itself.

The first respondent, the Chief Controller of Sales Tax, was appointed as an Assistant Commissioner of Sales tax in the State of Orissa. The first respondent was appointed by the Central Government as a Sales Tax Officer on ad hoc basis for a period of two years. He was later promoted as Additional Sales Tax officer. In the year 1973 he was served with a notice under section 9(2) of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be called upon to pay the tax due from him. The second respondent challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The High Court held that the first respondent had no locus standi to file the writ petition and quashed the order of the Central Govern ment on the ground that the law reports published by it were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the State Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable. The appellant filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court against the said judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by the Ist respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court and of the high Courts in India which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [778C] 1.2 In the instant case, the first Respondent has not been able to agree with the second respondent that the Law reports do not carry any news and that the public was not interested in them. The law report published by a Ist respondent contains information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme court or in the high courts which are Public bodies and those are matters of public importance. [779D] 1:3. In view of the fact that the expression 'newspaper ' as defined under the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news ', it is difficult to agree that the publication of the recent judgments itself is sufficient to make a law report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the legislation and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [780E F] 1 :4. The Law reports published in the law Reports of the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first appellant in their production or publication of such law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the central Government on that basis.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The agreement was described as an agreement of 'leave and licence ' entered into between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as the licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay. The licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the licensee had approached the licensor to allow him to occupy and use the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use the premises under the leave and licence of the licensor for a term of five year. The respondent filed an application for eviction on the ground that he was in occupation of the premises on 1st February, 1973 under a subsisting agreement for licence. The Small Cause Court held that the appellant was not a sub tenant but a licensee and not a tenant. The High Court allowed the revision on the view that there was no subsisting agreement between the parties and that the respondent was a tenant and having found that the period of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of this case it is a licence and not an agreement. good deal of submission was made before us that if it was a lease and not as a lease, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March, 1966 the leave & licence agreement between parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. The appellant 's contention that it was an agreement for leave and Licence was not supported by any evidence. good dealing of submission is made before this Court that if the exclusive possession to which a person was entitled under an agreement with a landlord was coupled with an interest in the property, the agreement would be construed not as mere licence but as a licence. good dealt of submissions were made before it that if there was any error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution. [231B C] 1.2 In view the background of the entire document evidencing the contention of the appellant that it is an agreement to leave and license, good deal o submission was submitted before this court that if this point had been taken in support of the plea that there were no subsisting contract for licence on the 1st of February 1973 as there was none on record, then the point could not be taken aid of. [232D] 1:3 In view Of the facts of this appeal and the background and the circumstances of the whole document evidencing its contention that the lease was not put an end to by the appellant and that in any event by filing the application for ejectment the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. This decision was remanded back to the High court and it is directed that the appeal be heard afresh in accordance with law because in a previous decision Vaidya, J. by the judgment dated 9th December, 1975 as mentioned hereinbefore had allowed the appellant ' s appeal.

The appellant company was incorporated in the State of Rajasthan. The Ruler of the Jodhpur State merged with the State Government and became a part of the covenanting State till such time as they were modified by the new State. On January 26, 1950, the Ruler of Jodhpur State transferred his rights to the Company under article 295(2) of the Constitution. In pursuance of this agreement the appellant company transferred its rights in favour of the Company on August 1, 1951 and on February 2, 1952, the Company was merged with it by virtue of the provisions of the Covenant. The Company continued to be a part B State of Madhya Pradesh till January 26. 1950. On March 12, 1952 the Ruler issued a notification under article 296(2), which provided that all the existing laws in the covenanted State shall continue until they were repealed or altered and the liabilities arising from the existence of those laws shall be the assets and liabilities of the Union. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the said notification on the ground that it was not in dispute that on January 26 1950, there was no recognition of the liability by the old State of Dholpur to; refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was made and that the liability did not devolve on the Part B State. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that article VI could not be enforced by citizens against the new sovereign as it emerged on January 1, 1950. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The agreement was not a law. It was part of an agreement between the Ruler and the Ruler. [184 D] (2) The covenant in the agreement was only a recognition of rights of subjects and that there was always recognition by the Union of India as regards the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always to this that if the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force.

The appellants were the sellers of certain agricultural crops in the State of Madras. The appellants were not prevented from doing their business, for they could still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. The State Government considered them and declared the areas to be specified in the notification or any portion thereof to be a notified area for the purpose of the Act. The appellant contended that the appellants had really two fundamental rights: one was to carry on trade or business and the other was to hold their property, i.e., the market; that by reason of the notification they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for them could still utilize it for commodity other than notified crops; and that the appellant had no right to do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also did business outside the prescribed area ; and that they were therefore not prohibited by bye laws framed under the Act, and that there was no violation of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the scheme of the bye law prohibiting the deduction of trade allowance and does not operate upon any other payments made which are not trade allowances. The object of the statute is to ensure that the market committee complies with the requirements of the law and it is not open to the Government to fix a long distance as a prohibited area; and so too, A, the seller may purport to sell one maund of cotton but in fact deduct a small part of it, retain that part for himself or give it to C. The question whether 'mahimai ' is a trade allowance depends upon the nature of that deduction. If on the other hand, mahimai ' was a deduction out of the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would not be a deduction from the price and commodity within the meaning of section 14 of The Act.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) There was no inconsistency between the two. There was a clear evidence that all the three lived together and that one was a younger brother and the other a tenant of the appellant in question. The fact that the appellants were also there but had no hand in the killing did not even hit him; and the High Court was right in holding that section 377 of the Code does not abrogate or modify that provision. (ii) There is no reason to depart from this practice in this case and so reduce the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia to transportation. The sentence should be reduced to transportation in these two cases also mainly because of the difference of opinion in the High Courts, not only on the question of guilt but also on that of sentence. (iii) There were no reasons to depart with this practice. (iv) There could be no doubt that the conviction was bad as there was no evidence to show that the accused had done anything except be present and even if it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow, at Ramchander 's thigh he was so half hearted about it that it did not Even hit him. (v) There can be no presumption of common intention in every case of murder under section 377 or section 378 of the Criminal Procedure Code that there is an element of common knowledge between the accused and the deceased. The distinction between a crime committed by a person and another was not a matter of law but one of fact, and it was common ground between them that the act must have been done in furtherance of the common intention of the accused. (vi) There are no compelling reasons to deviate from this rule in this connection.

The petitioner was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India and was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) after he had attained the age of 50 years. The petitioner challenged the said order before this Court on the ground that the order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner was promoted as officiating Executive Engineer which is a Class II post on 25.5.1972 and therefore on the date of the order he had completed the age Of 50 years, after he has attained the said age of fifty five years. [637C] 1.2 The object of Fundamental Rules 56(J) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Govern ment servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sory retirement is exercised, the Government Servant con cerned must be taken to be in Class I or Class II service or post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). [638E F] 1:3 The object and purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j) is that confer power upon the appropriate authori ty to compulsorily retired Government servant In the public interests and the classified categories covered under sub clauses(i) & (ii), has a vestige of discretion. If he is only a temporary hand, he has no right to the post and can always be reverted to the substantive post, if any, on which he has a lien. [625H; 626A] 1 :4 The object underlying Fundamental Rules 55(j) and 56( j) is not to confer powers on the appointing authority to compulsory retire Government servants in the Public interest and to bring about uniformity of treatment in respect of government servants who at the time of their appointment are in Class II or Class 11 service or posts, whether substantively, temporarily or on officiating basis. [ 626B] 1;5 The object is to conferring power on appropriate authority in the interest of public service and the differentiation between Government servants who have been appointed de novo may be justified by the purpose of sub clauses.(i) to (ii). If the officer is not in Class 11 or Class I service or Post, he had no right of the post. [ 625C] 2:6 The object for Fundamental Rules56(j), is to conferment power on Government servants to substantive posts in the Govern ment and the distinction between Government servant who are in class I or class II service and those who at that time are in classes I or classes 11 service, whether permanently or temporarily, on officiating or temporary basis. If a Government servant belonging to a Class I and Class II Service or post is in such service orpost as covered by subsection (i), he has an right to tho post and cannot be strictly said to be In that service or the post as a member of that service. [643E F; 626B C] 2.1 Sub clause (ii)(a) of Rule 56 of the Fundamental Rules, which is relevant for the purpose, is to give effect to the policy of the Government in regard to the conditions of service of government serv ers and other employees who are governed by sub cl.(i).

The appellant Corporation issued a notice to the respondent Corporation for payment of the amount of premium payable by it towards the first premium and also for payment thereof. The respondent Corporation did not pay the amount within the stipulated period. The appellant Corporation filed a suit against the respondent corporation for recovery of the sum of money paid by it, on the ground that there was a concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It was alleged that with full knowledge of the completion of all preliminaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the second premium and therefore it was the case of the plaintiffs respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal. The Trial Court held that there were no concluded contract of insurance between the appellant Corporation and the respondent. It also noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to the Corporation was not that the proposal was as a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Manager, on behalf of the Corporation, but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by the respondent without any demur or qualification and that in any event the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of proposal. It further held that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the corporation that the payment of first premium would amount to the acceptance of his proposal were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to acceptance of tho proposal if the proposal Was not otherwise accepted. The High Court also held that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was no concluded insurance contract between them and therefore the suit was maintainable. Allowing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the Corporation nor was it proved and secondly because there was nothing to show that such could have been the deposition in law. [359H; 360A] 1.2 In the instant case, the allegation that there is assurance on behalf by the field officers and local agent to the deceased that the payments of first premiums would amount acceptance of a proposal were neither established nor even if it was proved and lastly because there is no evidence that such can have been, the deposition of law. The allegation that the amount paid were appropriated towards the premium and the want of any further action to be done by the deceased did not itself create a contract of Insurance between the respondent and the corporation. [360B] 1:3 In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs in this Court.

The appellant, a company carrying on business in coal and coke oven plants, was granted a certificate of fitness under article 133(1)(a) of the Constitution. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of income tax dues from it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree holding that an order granting interim injunction "is final" and as such not appealable. In appeal to this Court, HELD: An order passed by the High 'Court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding is not final within the meaning of article 134(1) (c) since the controversy between the parties when the complaint in respect of offences under sections 467 and 468 read with section 114 I.P.C., could be filed against the appellant, it was held not to be final. [955 B] In the present case, the High court 's order refusing to grant an interim injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the parties in relation to the matter in dispute in the suit. The order refusing the interim injunction does not determine whether the order finally disposes of the rights of the party in dispute or not. [936 C] In view of the decision of this Court in Druva Coal Company vs Benaras Bank, ; , it is clear that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights or liabilities of the ' parties is not a judgment, however cardinal the issue may be. The test of finality according to the court is whether the decision on an issue put an end to the suit, the order will undoubtedly be a final one, but if after the order is made, the suit or proceedings still remain to be tried, and the rights in dispute have to be determined, the ' order is interlocutory. [946 D] In this case, it is not contended that the order of the High .Court amounts to a judgment or decree. The expression "final order" in article 133 (1) means an order which finally determines the points in controversy and brings the case to an end. The question whether an order finally disposing of the right of the plaintiff in dispute is final within article 134 (1)(c) of ' the Constitution has been decided by this Court. In the instant case, therefore, the trial court decided the issue against the respondent and the order was confirmed in appeal by the . High Court.

The petitioners, who were engaged in the manufacture of grey cloth, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the validity of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of 'the grey cloth in the hands of the processor plus the value as per the provisions of Rule 174 of the Rules. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessable value is the value at which the said manufacturer is selling the goods must be the price of the grey cloth or fabric plus the cost of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses. But if the trader who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be his price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessablevalue of the manufactured fabric and excise duty would be charged to the invoice on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at Which he would he selling the grey goods in his market, would include only the price or deemed price at that place. [346G H] 1.2 The value of a job work is not the value for purposes of Rule 173 of the rules. It is necessary to include the processor 's expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to mention the manufacturer 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [347A B] 1:3 The assessable values are the value in which the goods are manufactured by the processor. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value or deemed prices of the raw material in the shape of the finished product or fabric, plus the price cost of such job work performed plus manufac turing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It was necessary to included the processor "s profits" who gets his fabrics processed because those might be postmanufact profits. The value would be Rs.30, being the value on which he is selling these goods in market, and that would include also the cost or deemed value at that places. [348G H; 349A B C] 1 :4 Rule 174 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufacturedby another the information is required relating to the prices at which they said manufacturer was selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili tities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price atwhich he is sold must be, the value and the cost for the processing be Rs 5, then in such a case the value would include merely the price, or deemed sale price at the factory gate or deemed to be the assessable valuation of the goods. [349G H, 349A] 1 .5 The value for a job worked is not a value for purpose of Rule 172 of the Cen tral Excise Rules, 1944 but it was necessary in the instant case to include him 's profit.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On April 1, 1975 he was confirmed with effect from March 14, 1975. The appellant challenged his absorption on a lower post and filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by reason of section 14(4) of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1961 the appellant was entitled to continue in service of the Panchayat on the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the Panchayats Samiti until they were absorbed in Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head clerk in 1963, long before June 13, 1973, was not recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant had the right, to appoint him to the posts of Head Clerk or on April 1. [738C D] 2. The fact that the appellant is promoted as Head Clerk in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully to the Post of a clerk and that he is appointed lawfully does not alter his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13, 1972 when the amending Act came in force. [ 738E] 3. The order of the Government of Haryana notified the absorption of the appel lant as a Clerk though as stated earlier he was working as a head clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. He is therefore entitled to be absorbed in government service as a clerks in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 of the Act by the Amending act of 1973, the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The Government of Punjab notified the absorbing of the appellants as a junior clerk on April l, 1975 or the other fact that they were appointed as Head Clerks on April1, 1975 cannot improve his position.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity and that Mahant Shivshankar Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was decreed by the Civil Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati and Mahant Shivpher Yati. In appeal, the High Court held that Sadashiv Yati had not been a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saauna and Sarbakar of temple and that Sadasiv Yatti was not a regularly appointed Mahant of the temple and consequently, the Amauli properties must be regarded as his personal property and they did not belong to the institution or deity. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the income from the property was purchased by Mahant Ram Shivshanker Yati in 1921 from 662 the personal and separate funds inherited by him from his predecessor Shivphej Yati; (ii) the Amaul properties were described by Mahant SHIVshankar Yadav as properties of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from levy was made. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivsh Shankar Yatri and do not form part of the properties of Math or the temple; (iii) the liability of the Mahant Shiv Shanker Yati to tax was on the person who makes the claim. [657C D] 2. The High Court has found that the claim was not accepted by the assessing authority, and that the position in regard to those properties taken in the assessment proceedings was adopted by the Mahant only for the purpose of escaping personal liability to tax. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. They applied for quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. The Custodian General rejected their application on the ground that his jurisdiction to revise the order had been taken away by virtue of the provisions of , (44 of 1954) and the notification issued thereunder on March 24, 1955. The appellants then applied for restoration of the land to them which was refused by the Deputy Custodian General. The revision application filed by the appellants was rejected by the Custodian General on the view that his power to revise an order had not been taken over by virtue Of section 19 of the Act and the Notification issued thereunder. Held, that the Custodian 's power under the , to allot any property to a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. The power of the Custodian under the . to allot such property to persons or to cancel an allotment existing in favour of a person depends upon the facts of each case and it cannot be said that section 19(1) of the 1954 Act is completely in conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation of allotment is concerned. The effect of sections 12 and 19 of , is that the displaced person to whom land was allotted "held" the land and was in possession of such property at the date of the notification. The expression "held", therefore, means a managing agent or a managing corporation constituted under that Act. The word "held ' in section 19 (1) does not mean a mere manager or a Managing Agent but includes a managing agency. The words "held". and "held " are used in the context of the definition of "held property" in section 2(d) of . The expression 'held" is not defined in the Act. It is only when the word " held" is used that it would be an evacuee property. The definition of 'held property ' in the , includes a lease or a lease which is granted before the commencement of the , and does not include a lease. The term "held." means a lease, a lease etc., and not a lease for a period of more than one year. The fact that subsequent to the issue of the Notification under section 12(1), the property would cease to be evacuee property, the aforesaid powers of the custodian would be in conflict With those conferred by section 19 Of the 1954 , on a managing officer or a manage corporation constituted by that Act and could not rectify any error made by him in the past in the matter of cancellation.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women), District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Controllers of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Care) and DistrictHOK of Girls schools/Associates Regional Controllers, in Uttar pradesh. The advertisement inviting applications from qualified candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published by the State Government on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission cancelled the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that they had better performances in the selection process. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the oral examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. [125B] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a new interview of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final and would not be disturbed. The State Public Service commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not hail if the litigation could have reached. [126C D] 1:3 In the instant case, when no defect had been pointed out by the appellant, the High Court has upheld the actions of the public Service Commission and has dismissed the Writ Petitions. The selection of two Scheduled Castes candidates and 5 Backward Class candidate has become complete and would be in accordance with the interview part of recruitment and on the principle of equality of opportunity enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. [127F G] 1 :4 In the process, there is hardly any justification for cancellation of the written parts of the selection examina ble. The procedure adopted by the Public Commission has been completely misconceived and has resulted in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [128B C] 2.1 The situation can have been suitably met by set aside the selection and asking the for a second interview of only eligible candidates in accordance wit h the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. There is no justification to cancel the written Part of the Recruitment Examination and asking a fresh examination of all other eligible candidates. [129C D, E] 2:2 The State Government should have be more careful while dealing with matters so that 4 years in process of selection would not has been lost.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. The defendant contended that the Dhoti was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of properties of the dera as its lawful mahant; that the appellant had no right to recover possession of that property of the deceased Dera; that he had no locus standi to file the suit and that the suit was barred by limitation. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass, as his Chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy was raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the dead person within the time prescribed by law. The High Court also held that after S 's death, Shia Ram as his chela "Inherited, the sum of total of rights which already vested in the Dio could make no difference when he was elected as mahant of the S ' and that there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as a mahant to succeed him. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The suit was filed on the basis that the plaintiff as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of Dera at Landeke, that the defendant was unlawfully claiming to be the mahant and entitled to management the properties; and that he could be added as parties under Order 22, rule 10 notwithstanding that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. [490C] 2. The subject matter of the suit is the interest of Som Das in the S Dera. Som Dass. He was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of the Rera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as ma Mahant subsequent to the death, of Som Chand. [491D] 3. The question whether the interest in the subject matter was the interest or the property of a party in the C 's representative capacity or not depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. [492E] 4. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest, of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22 Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. [483G] 5. The rule that had to be apply is Order 21, rule 1, r. 10, and not Rule 3 or 5, whether devolution takesplace as a result of death, or for some other reason.[494C D] 6. When the suit has been brought by a party or against any person in representative capacity, there is no devolution of interest during the pendency of a suit and the elected persons can be added to as parties in order 22, Rule 10 notwithstanding the fact that the periods of limitation prescribed for impleading themselves under Order 21 rule 1 have expired. In Roshan Lal vs Kapur Chand the Court took the view that newly appointed trustees are not legal representatives or of the trustees who had filed the suit, and thereafter died during the course of the litigation, that they can be add as parties to under Order 2, Rule 3 notwithstanding the period that the limitation for impleaded them had elapsed. [504E] 7. The Court said that where some of the members die or retire during the proceedings of a case and new persons are elected to fill their place, it is a case of devolution of interests during the pending suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the court.

The petitioners, who were Government employees in the State of Andhra Pradesh, were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department on different dates between January 1, 1979 and October 29, 1979. The age of retirement was increased from 55 to 58 years by a notification dated October 29.8.1979. The petitioners challenged the reduction of their age of superannuation from 58 to 55. The Government of Andhra State issued a notification on September 17, 19,975 fixing the age of the employees as 55 and directing that the age should be increased from 58 years to 60. The State Government by its order dated October 16, 1979 fixed the age for retirement of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service, from 58 upto 58 years. The petitioner challenged the said notification on the ground that it was unreasonable. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the reduction was not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the Government had acted unreasonably in not giving any previous notice to the employees which would have enabled them to arrange their affairs on the eve of retirement; that the State Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which are relevant on the fixation of the age and, therefore, the decision taken by the Government was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the date of retirement. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution is not violative of Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary nor unreasonable in its circumstances. [723D] 2.1 The Government had taken a decision on its own to increase the age from 55 and 58 years, that the said recommendation was accepted by the State government and consequently, the age was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l 979. It is not therefore arbitrary or irrational in the facts of the present case. No. The contention of the petitioners is that the proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be changed retrospectively so as not to take away rights which had already accrued to them. [758E F] 2:2 The Government was therefore justified in its contention that arbitrary fixation of retirement age amounts to "removal" from service and is therefore violative of article 14 or 16 since the employees had acted on the representation made to them in 1979 by increasing the age Of retirement from 55 years to 58; that as a result of the increase in the age, of retirement from 58, to 55, the vested right had accrued to the petitioners, which could be taken away, if at all, only from future entrants to the Government service; and that the decision of the Government is bad for any total non Application of mind. [759E F G] 2 :3 The Government has acted unreasonably without giving any prior notice to employees who had already been stagnated in the lower positions due to expansion of educational facilities; that, the present measure was intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees whose number was increasing enormously due to increase in age of Retirement from 55to 58 years; that it would take welfare measures in order to improve the lot of the common man, and. particularly, in orderto afford opportunities to qualified and talented unemployed youths whose number is increasing enormally due to increased expansion of education from 55 To 58; and, the Government employees were stagnated by the increase of the ages of retirement, which was due to the increase being caused by expansion of Educational facilities; and the present action was intended for reducing the age.

The Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 was enacted to provide for the levy of purchase tax on goods other than those specified in Schedule B. Section 9(1) provides that where a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act, fails to make payment of tax at the first stage of sale under section 17 or section 18, he shall pay the tax payable by him in respect of the tax due from him in accordance with the provisions of section 9. The appellants who were dealers in raw materials in the State of Haryana entered into agreements with certain other dealers for the purchase of raw materials and sold them to dealers who in turn exported those goods out of India. On these facts, the Sales Tax Officer issued a notice u/s 9(2) of the Act to the appellants on the ground that they were liable to tax under section 9(i)(b). The appellants challenged the validity of the said notices before the High Court and contended that since the sales effected by them fell within one of the three exempted categories set out in section 9 (1) of Act, the same was not taxable. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) Section 9 (i)(a) does not provide for levy of tax on the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is leviable under section 8 or section 9, and (ii) the expression "disposes of" used in clause (b) is inclusive. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "dispose of" in clause(a)(ii) of sub section (1), are wide enough to include cases where raw materials were purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the State to any place outside it". The words 'disposes the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter state trade or commerce" are wide and include cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufacturedgoods otherwise than under section 5(3). [362B C] 2.1 The expression "dealers" is defined in Section 2(p) as including persons who were not specified in schedule B, except milk, from any source in the state and uses them in the said State in the manufacture of any other goods and either disposed of the manufac tured goods to the dealer or used them in his own way. [362C D] 2:2 The expression 'disposal of" is wide enough and includes within the definition of "turnover". The word 'turnover ' has been defined in s.2(c), as meaning the taking out from the goods by a person who purchases them from the market, to a places outside the state in any way otherwise than for by way off sale in tho course of Inter State trade or business. [363D E] 2 :3 The definition also excludes from its purview "disposals" other than "in the course ' of inter State trade and commerce". [362E] 3.1 In the instant case, the sales were effected by the assessees fall within one or more exempted categories. There can be no doubt that a tax is levied under the Act on the goods in question when they are sold by a registered dealer for the purpose of export outside the territory of India within the meaning of sub s.(1) and sub section 2 of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax, 1956. [361H; 362A] 3:2. The language of section 8(1)(a)(i) is wide and includes cases where goods are disposed of only by way o sale in inter Statetrade or in the inter State outside the territories of India, within the ambit of sub sec tion (1). [363B C].

The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948. He sold his goods to the respondent who in turn sold them to the appellant. The respondent filed a return of sales tax on the ground that the sales were not their property till they crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales could be exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that the transactions were not liable to purchase tax under section 10(b). On further appeal, the High Court held that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales had been oncart track property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered person and the purchasing dealer does not show to the satisfaction of the Collector that the articles have been despatched by him or by a person to whom he has sold the goods. The words " the person who has given such certificate" in section 8(b) mean "a registered dealer to whom the certificate has sold it". The words 'the person who is not a registereddealer ' are wide and they do not include a person who does not have any special agreement with the purchasing dealers that the article should be despatched by a registered dealers. The word " registered dealer" in the section means a registered under the Act. The expression "a Registered dealer" has been defined in section 2(g) of that Act to mean a registered registered dealer. The definition of " registered dealers" is wide enough and it includes a person whose name is not registered. The fact that the certificate is issued by the purchasingdealer does not make any difference. The certificate is only a registered one and the purchase is made by a Registered dealer.

The appellant, a married woman, was married to the respondent on April 1, 1962. The appellant had transferred her suit premises to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The respondent filed an application under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. The magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for the mother for their subsistence, taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the Appellant. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract section 125 and his third contention was that there was a settlement by consent decree in 1962 whereby the appellant had been divorced by her husband and that he had received, whether before or after the date of the said order, the whole of the sum which, under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties, was payable on such divorce cancel such order, (i) in the case where such sum was paid before such order from the date on which such order was made. (ii) in any other case from the day of expiry of the period if any for which maintenance has been actually paid by the husband to the woman; and (iii) in a case where the husband, by customary payment at the time of divorce, has adequately provided for the divorce, a subsequent series of recurrent does is 81 contra indicated and the husband liberated. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Courts below had grave errors of law apparent on the face of record. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not entitled to any allowance. [81G] 1.2 In a case of divorcee under section 127(3) (b), it is clear that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. The legal sanctity of the payment is certified by the fulfilment of the social obligation, not by a ritual exercise rooted in custom. If the first payment by way of mehar or ordained by custom has a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section125 not mathematically but wholly. [82A] 1:3 The legal status created as a projection of public policy by the Code of 1973, which could not have been in the contemplation of the parties when in 1962, they entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. No settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of the divorcee Under section 125 can operate to extinguish that claim. Payment of meherhar money, as a customary discharge, is within the cognisance of that provision. [83B] 1 :4 The legal efficacy of the payments is certifiedby the fulfilment Of the social obligations, not through a ritual exercising rooted In custom. But where the wife, by custom, has adequate means to obviate destitution of the marriagee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. The purpose of payment 'under any customary law' must be to obviate perspectives of the husband and is to obviate compassion of the separatione and To provide her With wherew aids to maintain themselves are more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance. The concept, therefore, is that no husband can claim under section 126(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section 124 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or Personal law whose quantum is more or greater than sufficient to discharge duty for Maintenance allowance. If any in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill used wife and the derelict divorcee, her husband liberate.

The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 under which he was directed to black list the appellant. The said order was challenged by the State Government in a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the black listing of the appellant was not specifically mentioned in the order and that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the State that there is no requirement specifically of giving any notice under the rule of giving an opportunity to the appellant as he had been given a show cause notice and that the cancellation of the bid of the appel lant was not justified. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing order passed by the Collector is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not affected. This order will, however, not prevent the State Govt. or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps for cancelling the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law. [868C D] 1.2 The order of the Collector dated 25th 3 1988 is set out in verbatim below: "Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Thakur, Village Repura, P.S. Puksha, District Samastipur has bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Singh S/O Late Gorakh Nath Village Repudwara, Pages. 1.3 The cancellation of bid of appellant is concerned. That is not effected. [886D E] 2. The order dated 25.3 1988 of the Collec tor is set quashed. So long as the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing the appellant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law.

The appellant was the landlord of a house in Madras. The respondent landlord filed an application under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises leased to him. The Rent Controller rejected the application on the ground that the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant site and not a vacant land. On appeal, the High Court held that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to fix the fair rent under section 64 C which was applicable only to the vacant site. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that since the subject Matter of the leased property originally formed part of an extent of land and the Rent Control Act was not applicable, the Rent controller had no juris diction to fix such fair rent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether a landlord is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and (2) what the fair rental of the property should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act is only a determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. [550G] 1.2 In view of the finding that the lease in question was only an vacant site, the question on which the jurisdiction of the Rent control ler under the Act was excluded is only the determination as regards the fair and standard rent of the building. If the Rent Authority did not decide that question properly, the matter would have to be raised in appeal to the Court of Small Causes and would give this Court no jurisdiction. [552B C] 1:3. The question on the question whether the order in the earlier rent control proceedings decided to the contrary and fixing the fair standard rent is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent Court under the Tamil nadu Act. [553C D] 1 :4. The terms of section 64 of the Madras Buildings (lease and Rent) Control)Act, 1960 are not decisive on the point of ouster of the civil court 's jurisdiction. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the rent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the proper rent is and then fades out of picture. In such a case, the tenant would be entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the landlord on the basis of the fair rents fixed by the Rent Act. If and only when this relationship existed between the par ties, the landlord steps in seeking eviction of the tenant on the strength of the valid lease deed. [554D E] 1 5. The Court has to decide whether the applicant is a 'tenant ' or not. If it does not decide the question properly so, the decision will be final and binding.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the High Court. The petition er challenged the final inter State seniority list on the ground that he was not heard after the final list was prepared. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the case now before it is governed by what was held by this Court in Shankariah 's case with reference to an entirely different and provisional list of Forest Officers. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner respondent was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him before the final seniority list was to be declared and published as a final list. [838E] 1.2 In order to establish the invalidity of the final gradation list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. The decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration ation, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts. [828G] 1:3 In order that a particular judge may go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government, it would necessarily be fair to give a person affected an 'oppo rtunity to be heard against the proposed list before it was finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts, may be rectified. [829B C] 1 :4 The petitioner re spondent was claiming relief against the final Inter State seniority List although he was given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. He is a respondent before us. [827E F] Shankariah vs Union of India, ; , followed.

The appellant company was manufacturing and selling the goods in packed condition. The packing material was to be supplied by the buyer to the assessee at the factory gate. The containers were not returnable by the buyers, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. The appellant contended that on a correct interpretation of section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act, the cost of packing could be included In the assessable Value only when the packing is either manufactured by the assessee or is purchased by the asses see to the buyer, in respect of all other costs of packing, the costs should be included. The Revenue contended that the value of packing materials including those supplied by it had to he included in its assessable value only when they were sold at the time of removal in packed conditions and the containers were therefore not returnable to by the purchaser, there was no reason for the appellant to include the cost incurred by the manufacturer when the pack is supplied by him. The Tribunal held that the cost price of packing envisaged in section 4 (4)(D)(i), did not in clude within its ambit the cost for packing not incurred by it when the containers are supplied by a buyer and not the manufacturer, and therefore, the sale value had also to be excluded from the assessable valuation. The revenue appealed to this Court against the Tribunal 's order. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 In cases where the Act provides for excise duty with reference to value of the excisable goods, while determining the value, of such goods, the Cost of packing where the excisable article is delivered at the place of removal, in packed Condition, would have to be added to the price except where the packing was of durable nature and returnable to the manufacturer. The "cost of such pack ing" referred in section4(4) (d)(ii) does not in elude within their ambit the costs of pack ing not incurred wholly by the manufacturers when the packed is supplied at the depot gate. [982A] 1.2 In cases, where the statute provides for duty with respect to value, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. In this view of the matter, it is unnecessary to discuss wider questions as to the circumstances in which the cost o packing (primary or secondary) can at all enter into the determination of the assessablevalue under section 4.(4)(c)(i). [987C D] Union of India & Ors. vs Godfrey Phillips, by the learned Attorney General. [1989] Suppl. 1 S.C.R. 981; Union of lndia vs Godafrey Philips, ; , referred to. 1.3 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amend ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value", the nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that, while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at a factory gate is to be taken as the assessable values, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the sale price, the manufacturers levies a charged for the pack ing which is 475ically and necessarily incidental to placed placing the finished product on the Market. [990D E] Union Of India & Anr. vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., ; , followed.

The appellant was charged with having committed the offence of running a canteen in the State of Tamil Nadu. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued, stopped it. He was alleged to have pressed the demand to PW 1, who on 21.10.1975 informed him that he would help him in restoring the licence and demanded a bribe of Rs. 100. On 21. 10.1975, the appellant was stated to have made a complaint to PW I, the Chief Inspector of the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. The appellant was examined by PW 1 on 21 10 1975 itself. He had admitted that he had pressed the demands to PW l, but later on he gave the money to him. The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant has not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient to hold that the money was paid and there had been no demand for a bribe as there had already been no demands for a sum of Rs 100. The High Court took the view that the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is incon sistent with the transaction of loan or return of money by PW l. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption arising under section 4(1) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act which has not be en rebutted. [337B] 1.2 In a case where the existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to be rebutted. The presumption created in section 4 of the Act has not to be displaced by mere preponderance of probabilities. [340D] 1:3. In State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; , this Court observed that though the conviction under section 5 of the prevention of Corruption is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., the presumption has to be rebut ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to he proved when its existence is indirectly directly established, or when on the material date that finds its strength to be unreasonable. [341E F] 1 :4. In a given case, where the prosecution witnesses are unable to prove affirmatively rebutting their presumption, the court has no choice in the matter.
