The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was created by the name of Sakharam Maharaj at Amalner in the year 1817, and installed the deity according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the same were held by him as his own property. The appellant 's case was that he was the owner of the property and that he had been using it for Darshan by the public. The Assistant Charity Commissioner by his order dated August 25, 1956, held that the Sansthan to be a public trust and not a public religious endowment. The High Court in revision set aside the order of the District Judge and restored the order passed by the Charity Commissioner. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the temple was a private property and it was also transferred to the Shishya Adhikari to maintain it as his personal property; that there was absolutely no evidence of any restriction in the matter of continuous worship by the Public or public user of the temple as a matter of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole; and that the High Court had wrongly held that there were no evidence to show that the appellant was in any way concerned with the management of the Sansthan. HELD: (i) The High court was not right in giving due importance to the admission of the constituted attorneys about the nature of the endowment by the appellant. [519 B] (ii) The order passed on August 25 1956, was a document which was relied upon both by the District judge as well as the High court. It was a deed of nomination by three businessmen of Amalmer and the appellant 'was appointed as the Treasurer in order to take charge of the properties. The trust was created for the worship and maintenance of Sri Jagannath Maharaj. The temple was dedicated to the appellant for the Darshan by public. [525 C D] (iii) The appellant had been given a full picture of the working of the temples, and he was not entitled to any protection under article 19(1)(g). [521 G] (iv) The temple in its own name was recipient of land by Royal grant and the said right was taken away by the Government in favour of the Temple or the Sansthan for the purpose of maintenance of worship. [500 E] (v) The fact that the deity installed in the temple is not conclusive evidence of the restriction in question on the temple being a public temple.

The petitioner was arrested and detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 for the recovery of the demand certified under section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner contended that (i) section 46 (2) Of the Indian Incometax Act offended article 14 of the Constitution and (ii) that section 13 Of the Bombay Provincial Land Revenue Code, 1879 was violative of article 22(1) and (2), article 14 and article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of all the State laws are mutatis mutandis to be read into section 46 of the Act and that therefore if there be any vice of discrimination in the State law that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section46(2). The grouping of the income tax defaulters into separate categories or classes Statewise is certainly a territorial classification which is based on an intelligible differentia and the subjection, for the purposes of the recovery Of their own public demands, cannot be regarded by itself as bereft of a reasonable nexus or correlation between the basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian income tax Act any more than it can be so regarded with respect to the respective State laws. The group making of the Income tax defaulters in separate categories and classes State wise is certainly one territorial classification, which is founded on an differentia and that the sub rejection, for, the purposes Of recovery of their own Public demands, could not be regarded 'as bereft of any reasonable nexus nor correlation between tho basis of discrimination and the objects sought to he achieved by it. The Indian Income Tax Act by section 46 has been amended and the warrant of detention was issued on the 7th June 1955, that is to say, long after the amendment of the section. The nature of the tax is one and the same, and it is levied under a single Central Act, and yet the ultimate coercive processes for recovery differ in nature and extent between State and State.

The respondents were the owners of a Port Trust, who were employed in the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents were paid wages at the time of the initial appointment and the same was fixed at Rs. 10,000/ per month. The Trustees of the Port Trust claimed that under a scheme of 12hour shift with 8 hours ' work, overtime should be at least 3 hours if not 4 hours in the case of an adult, 9 hours ' working day. The Tribunal held that the respondents were entitled to a 12 hours ' shift and rejected their claim for a fixed period of rest. On appeal by special leave: Held, that on any single day the number of hours of work must not exceed 9 and together with the hours of rest the total period of work and rest should not go beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 13(2) (c) read with section 13 (3) give an indication of what is meant by an interval of rest and give an impression of what was meant by the interval of time. The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a normal working day because the total number of work hours in a week cannot go beyond 48. The workers are entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours on any day. In a 12 hour shift, the nine hours of duty on anyday can be spread over 10 days and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of the rest. The provision of section 15(2)(c) of the Act does not itself fix the hours for rest but only fixes the hours in case of a adult, and it is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest; and if there is difficulty in giving the intervals for rest in that manner on any particular day, it cannot be said that the interval for rest shall break up the hours.

The appellant was the owner of a house let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and thereafter the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection under this Act. The landlord filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment of the appellant on the ground that apart from the controversy about the date which should be the starting point for computing the period of 10 years in view of the language of Sections 39 and 40 of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent & Eviction) Act, 1972, provisions of this Act will be applicable to the present case and therefore a decree for eviction could only be passed. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the revision petition set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as during the pendency of this matter in this Court 10 years have not been completed and therefore the High court passed the decree Now it could not be contended that as till the matter was pending in the High Courts, 10 years had elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1. In view of this the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 20 of the Act because according to him the appeal will be a continuation of the suit and therefore he advantage will be available. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right of the parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date when the suit was filed. But in Vineet Kumar 's case (supra) this Court took the view that if during the course of proceedings 10 years has elapsed the tenant is entitled to benefit of Section 2 restriction of the institution of suit as provided for in Section 20 clause (1) quoted above will not be applicable and it is thus clear that during the period 1.10.86, 10 year have to be computed from 1.12.87 but this contention could not been accepted as it was very clear from the language used in the said provision that it applied only to a suit pending on the day of commencement of the . [167F H] 1.2 The appellant tenant cannot claim protection under Section 20 because of the wording of Section 39 and section 40 even if he is entitled for the benefit under this section even if his case is pending in this court. [167C D] 1:3 In the instant case, the suit giving rise to the instant appeal was filed on 23rd March, 1974 long after the commencement of this Court and therefore restriction as provided in Section 2 restrictions of the Institution of suit is not attracted and it was thus clear from a reading of Section 40 that it applies only to suits pending on that date. [168E F] 1 :4 The contention advanced by the appellant that because of language of Section39 and 40 even assuming that the matter is pending before this Court in this case, and 10 years having elapsed, the appellant will be entitle to the advantage of the Section even if it is held that the rights of parties have to he determined in respect of the date on which the suit is filed still because of this language of section 39 and the appellant is entitled only to the benefits of the provision of this Section. [169F G] 1 .5 The contention of the learned counsel could not therefore be accepted as the matter has been pending in that Court and 10 year has elapsed, i.e., 10 years. It is no doubt true that the appeal is the continuation of a suit and if within the language Of Section 39 the appellant 's right will be governed by the provisions even if this point is pending. [170G H] Om Prakash Gupta vs Smt.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment of the appellant tenant on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as amended by the West Bengal Thika Amendment Act, 1952. The trial court held that the tenancy of the respondent was governed by the Thika Tenant 's Protection Act, 1950 and the definition of a thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On appeal the High Court held that at the time when the appeal of the defendant was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by Thika Tenants ' Protection Act of 1950 and that the definition was not retrospective only because the landlord had not filed a plaint in accordance with section 3 of the Act but also under section 4 of the Ordinance. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant tenant that (i) the provisions of the Thiyka Tenancy Acts were prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord could not be said to have failed to establish his existence; (ii) the tenancy in question was governed under the Thirika Tenants Protection act of 1950 which came into force on 21st October before the commencement of the West Benares Thika Thika ' Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952 and therefore section 4 Of the Act would be applicable. HELD: (i)(a) The provisions of section 4 and 5 being prospective and not as such applied to pre existing suits, they were inapplicable to the pre existing suit. [519 C] (b) Section 4 of Act was prospective only and it could not apply to this case. [525 E] (c) The correct view is that sections 4 and 6 being prospective, the landlords had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. [511 F] (d) The right of the landlord to eject a thikka tenant after the Act had come into force could not therefore be said that he was entitled to protection under the Act as amended.

The appellants were appointed as Section Officers in the secretariat of the State of U.P. on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were promoted to the post of Section Officer by an order dated July 2, 1976. The appellants challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and directed the State Government to give them pay scale equal to Section Officers or Private Secretaries. Aggrieved by the aforesaid order, the appellants filed a Writ Petition in the High court which was dismissed. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the principle of "equal pay for equal work" has no application to the case of the petitioners; (ii) the Court had not agreed with the classification made under the Rules, and (iii) the High Courts were in error in holding that the State Govern ment had granted uniform pay scale of Rs. 1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Secretaries. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of 'equal pay ' for equal Work has to be construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge ing with the adminis tration in fixing pay scales has to he left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [306G H] 2. The High Court had completely overlooked the criterion provided under the rules, the merit governs the grant of higher pay scales and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification made tinder the Rules cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for Equal work. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our attention that the Court Secretaries Grade I are selected by a Selection Committee. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay Scale. [307D E] 3. The State Government has granted uniform Pay scale of pay of Rs 1600 2900 to both these grades of Judges with effect from January 1, 1986. It is against this background that the principle has to been construed in first place.[308G H; 308A] 4. One can deny that sometimes the difference was a matter which of degree or that there was an elementof value judgmentby those who were charged with administration in fixation of pay scales have to be left with him and it could not be interfered by the court unless it was demonstrated that neither it is wholly irrational nor based on any basis or arrive mala fide, either in fact or in law. [308C] 5. The Court Secretaries, therefore cannot claim as of right the pay scale admissible to Section officers. The question is whether there can be two scales of Pay in the same cadre of persons performing the same or similar work or duties. The Bench Secretaries Grade 1 are selectedby a Selection Commis sioner. The Rules thus make it a proper selection for the purposes of entitlement for higher pay ment scale. [309D E; 308F] 6. The pay scale recommended by the Pay Commission is as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 50 two posts of Bench Secretary Grade II and the posts of Benches Secretaries Grade III and the post in the scale of ` Rs.500 1,000. The Committee Secretaries Grade II are selected from a Selection committee. The qualifications for appointment to the posts are prescribed by Rule 4(1)(a) of the Rules.

The respondent, a sugar undertaking owned by the appellant, was granted mining lease in respect of certain lands situated in the area of village Khedpur. The appellant, who was the owner of the said land, had applied for mining leases in respect thereof. The respondent 's application was rejected on the ground that the appellant had waived its right to carry on business under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1956 and the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act 1961. The High Court held that the respondent was incompetent to exercise the powers of the Municipality or the Municipal Corporation had no competence to levy any tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the aforesaid Acts. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the State Legislature had no power to pass a law on the subject and the State legislature had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The legislative power of the State under Entry 24 List II was eroded only to the extent to which control was assumed by the Union Government pursuant to the declaration made by Parliament in respect for a declared industry and that the field occupied by such enactment was the measure of the erosion of the legislative competence of the state legislature. [23C D] 2. The power conferred by the State Legislatures on Special Area Development Authorities to impose the property tax on lands and buildings is therefore not in conflict with the power conferred under Section 69(d) of the Act of 1973. It was held by this Court that the legislative power under Entry 52 List I, was erived only to Parliament and that, the ownership rights could be validly acquired by the Government under the State Act. [24D E] 3. It provides that the property Tax shall not be leviable inter alia on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union government". The property taxes are imposed by Respondent 1 under Section 127A(2) of Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1951 or the Madhya Madhya Pradesh Panchayats Act, 1961. [25E F] 4. The State Legislature has no competence either to pass any law on a subject and to the State Government pursuant pursuant to declaration made in respect under section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957. It is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under Section69(d). [26G] 5. The land tax is levied by respondent I under section 126A of Madhya Bharat Panchayats Act and Section 135 of Municipal Corporation Corporation Act respectively. [27H; 27A] 6. The appellant was the lessee of a mining lease granted to him by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was in for a term exceeding one years it was enforceable against him. The appellant filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground that the Government had no power under section 20 (1) to terminate the lease. The High Court held that the words " such rights" in the third proviso to sub section (2) of section 20 were not intended to refer to the rights created after July 1 1945, mentioned in the previous proviso and on that construction the lease in favour of the appellant could be terminated only in accordance with that proviso by giving three months ' notice. The question for determination was whether the termination of the lease by the Board of revenue was valid or not. Held, that the word "such rights" used in the second sub section must mean those created before the notified date but after July1, 1945 for a periods exceeding one month would be valid and enforceable both by and against the State Government. The words "such right" in section 20 of the Act are wide enough to include all rights created before that date but they cannot be limited only to those created after the 1st July, 1945.
